sections.body:
Julia evaluates what you type and shows the value of the last expression, just
like the REPL (the `julia>` prompt you get by running `julia`). The sandbox
on this site does the same: press **Run** and you see what the REPL would
print.

Arithmetic works the way you expect, with one thing to notice early: `/`
always produces a floating-point number, even when both sides are integers.
Use `÷` (type `\div` then Tab) or `div` for integer division, and `%` for the
remainder.

examples.caption: `/` returns a Float64 even for integers; `÷` keeps integers.
examples.code:
println(7 / 2)
println(7 ÷ 2)
println(7 % 2)
6 / 3

sections.title: Everything is an expression

sections.body:
A variable is a name bound to a value; `x = 3` binds `x`. Variables do not
have types, *values* do, and `typeof` tells you which. On a 64-bit machine an
integer literal is an `Int64`, a literal with a decimal point is a `Float64`,
text in double quotes is a `String` and a single character in single quotes is
a `Char`.

When you mix types in arithmetic, Julia *promotes* to a common type: `Int64`
plus `Float64` is a `Float64`. Names can use Unicode, which is common in
scientific code: type `\alpha` then Tab to get `α`.

examples.code:
x = 3
y = 2.5
println(typeof(x), " ", typeof(y), " ", typeof(x + y))
println(typeof("hi"), " ", typeof('h'), " ", typeof(true))
examples.output:
Int64 Float64 Float64
String Char Bool

examples.caption: Rebinding a name to a value of another type is allowed (but inside functions it can cost speed; see the performance unit).
examples.code:

α = "now a string"
typeof(α)

sections.title: Variables and the types of values

sections.body:
`println` prints its arguments and a newline; `print` does not add the
newline. Inside a string, `$name` inserts the value of a variable and
`$(expression)` inserts the value of any expression. The macro `@show` prints
an expression together with its value, which helps while debugging.

A trailing `;` on the last line hides the value, as in the REPL.

One trap: `!` is allowed in names (`push!` is a function), so `"$name!"`
looks for a variable called `name!`. Write `"$(name)!"` instead.

examples.code:
name = "Ada"
born = 1815
println("Hello, $(name)! You were born in $born, $(2025 - born) years before 2025.")
print("no newline, ")
print("so this continues the line")
println()
@show born * 2;
examples.output:
Hello, Ada! You were born in 1815, 210 years before 2025.
no newline, so this continues the line
born * 2 = 3630

sections.body:
An integer literal is an `Int64` (on a 64-bit machine `Int` is another name
for `Int64`). It holds 64 bits, so there is a largest and a smallest value:
`typemax(Int)` and `typemin(Int)`.

Going past the largest value does **not** raise an error and does not switch
to a bigger type, as Python does. The arithmetic *wraps around*: one more than
`typemax(Int)` is `typemin(Int)`. Julia does this on purpose, because checking
every addition would make all integer code slower. Powers wrap too: `2^63`
is one past `typemax(Int)`, so it comes out as `typemin(Int)`, and `2^64`
needs 65 bits, so what is left in 64 bits is `0`.

Smaller types such as `Int8` (−128 to 127) wrap the same way, just sooner.

examples.code:
println(typemax(Int))
println(typemin(Int))
println(typemax(Int) + 1)
println(2^63)
println(2^64)

examples.caption: An `Int8` wraps after 127. Arithmetic between two `Int8`s stays `Int8`.
examples.code:
x = Int8(127)
y = x + Int8(1)
println(y, " ", typeof(y))

sections.title: Integers have a fixed size and wrap around

sections.body:
A `Float64` stores a number in binary with about 16 significant decimal
digits. Most decimal fractions, like `0.1`, have no exact binary form, so
`0.1 + 0.2` is not exactly `0.3` and `==` says `false`. This is the same in
every language that uses IEEE floating point (Python, MATLAB, R, C).

Compare floats with `≈` (type `\approx` then Tab), which is `isapprox`: equal
within a relative tolerance. Close to zero a *relative* tolerance is useless
(nothing is relatively close to 0), so pass an absolute one with `atol`.
`eps()` is the gap between `1.0` and the next float.

examples.code:
println(0.1 + 0.2)
println(0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3)
println(0.1 + 0.2 ≈ 0.3)
println(1e-20 ≈ 0.0)
println(isapprox(1e-20, 0.0; atol = 1e-12))
eps()

println(0 / 0)
println(1 ÷ 0)

sections.title: Floating point is approximate

sections.body:
`÷` (`\div`) and `div` divide and **truncate toward zero**; `%` and `rem` give
the matching remainder, which has the sign of the *dividend*. `fld` rounds
toward minus infinity (floor) and `mod` gives the matching remainder, which has
the sign of the *divisor*. `cld` rounds up (ceiling).

For positive numbers `÷`/`fld` and `%`/`mod` agree. With a negative number they
do not, as the table shows. If you come from Python: Python's `//` is `fld`
and Python's `%` is `mod`, not Julia's `%`. Use `mod` for "wrap into the
range `0:n-1`" (clock arithmetic, circular indexing).

examples.code:
for (a, b) in ((7, 2), (-7, 2), (7, -2))
    println("a = $a, b = $b:  a ÷ b = ", a ÷ b, ",  a % b = ", a % b,
            ",  fld = ", fld(a, b), ",  mod = ", mod(a, b), ",  cld = ", cld(a, b))
end

examples.caption: `divrem` returns the quotient and remainder together; `mod` wraps negative positions back into range.
examples.code:
println(divrem(-7, 2))
println(fldmod(-7, 2))
println(mod(-1, 12), " ", mod(13, 12))

sections.title: Integer division and remainders with negative numbers

sections.body:
`//` builds a `Rational`: an exact fraction, always stored in lowest terms.
Rationals never round, so `1//10 + 2//10 == 3//10` is `true`.

`BigInt` is an integer of unlimited size; `big(x)` converts a number to it.
Use it when results really exceed 64 bits. It is much slower than `Int`
(every operation allocates memory), so do not use it "just in case".
Some functions refuse to overflow silently: `factorial(21)` does not fit in an
`Int64`, and `factorial` says so instead of wrapping.

examples.code:
x = 1//3 + 1//6
println(x, " ", typeof(x))
println(1//10 + 2//10 == 3//10)
println(numerator(6//8), " ", denominator(6//8))

println(big(2)^100)
println(typeof(big(2)^100))
println(factorial(big(25)))
factorial(21)
examples.output:
1267650600228229401496703205376
BigInt
15511210043330985984000000
ERROR: OverflowError: 21 is too large to look up in the table; consider using `factorial(big(21))` instead
  @ top-level scope at line 4

sections.title: Exact arithmetic: Rational and BigInt

sections.body:
Calling a type as a function, `Int(x)`, converts *exactly or not at all*:
`Int(2.0)` is `2`, but `Int(2.5)` throws an `InexactError` because 2.5 is not
an integer. The same goes for values out of range, like `Int8(200)`.

To get an integer from a float that is not whole, say how to round:
`round(Int, x)`, `trunc(Int, x)` (toward zero), `floor(Int, x)` (down) or
`ceil(Int, x)` (up). Without the type they return a float. Notice that
`round` breaks ties to the *even* neighbour: `round(2.5)` is `2.0`, while
`round(3.5)` is `4.0`.

examples.code:
println(Int(2.0))
println(round(Int, 2.7), " ", trunc(Int, -2.7), " ", floor(Int, -2.7), " ", ceil(Int, -2.7))
println(round(2.5), " ", round(3.5), " ", round(-2.5))
println(float(3), " ", Float64(1//4))
Int(2.5)
examples.output:
2
3 -2 -3 -2
2.0 4.0 -2.0
3.0 0.25
ERROR: InexactError: Int64(2.5)
  @ top-level scope at line 5

ERROR: InexactError: trunc(Int8, 200)
  @ top-level scope at line 1

sections.title: Converting between number types

sections.body:
When an operation mixes types, Julia *promotes* both arguments to a common type
that can represent them and then computes in that type: `Int` and `Float64`
give `Float64`, `Int` and `Rational` give a `Rational`, a `Rational` and a
`Float64` give `Float64`. `promote` shows the result of that step.

Mixing an `Int8` with an `Int` gives an `Int`; the small type does not
"win". This is why you rarely need to convert by hand before arithmetic.

examples.code:
println(typeof(1 + 2.0))
println(1 + 1//2)
println(1//2 + 0.25)
println(typeof(Int8(1) + 1))
promote(1, 2.5, 3//4)

sections.body:
Double quotes make a `String`, single quotes make a `Char` (one Unicode
character). They are different types: `"a" == 'a'` is `false`. A `Char` is a
code point, so `'a' + 1` is `'b'`.

Julia joins strings with `*`, not `+` (in algebra `*` is the operation that
need not commute, like joining text), and repeats them with `^`. `string(...)`
converts and joins any values, and interpolation with `$` (unit 1) is usually
the clearest way to build text.

examples.code:
println(typeof("a"), " ", typeof('a'))
println("a" == 'a')
println('a' + 1)
println("Hello, " * "world" * "!")
println("ab"^3)
println(string("x = ", 42, ", y = ", 2.5, ' ', :done))

String Char
false
b
Hello, world!
ababab
x = 42, y = 2.5 done

sections.title: String and Char, and building strings

sections.body:
Julia strings are UTF-8. ASCII characters take one byte, but `é` takes two
(other characters up to four). A string index is a **byte position**, so for text with
non-ASCII characters not every integer is a valid index: `s[3]` below lands in
the middle of `é` and throws a `StringIndexError`.

`length(s)` counts characters, `ncodeunits(s)` counts bytes. To move between
characters use `eachindex(s)` (all valid indices), `nextind(s, i)` and
`prevind(s, i)`, and `firstindex`/`lastindex` instead of `1` and `length(s)`.
`s[end]` is safe: `end` means `lastindex(s)`.

examples.code:
s = "héllo"
println(length(s), " characters, ", ncodeunits(s), " bytes")
println(s[1], " ", s[2], " ", s[4], " ", s[end])
println(collect(eachindex(s)))
println(nextind(s, 2))
s[3]
examples.output:
5 characters, 6 bytes
h é l o
[1, 2, 4, 5, 6]
4
ERROR: StringIndexError: invalid index [3], valid nearby indices [2]=>'é', [4]=>'l'
  @ top-level scope at line 6

examples.caption: A byte range slice works when both ends are valid indices: `naïve` is 6 bytes. Ending inside `ï` (byte 4) is an error.
examples.code:
s = "naïve café"
println(s[1:6])
println(s[lastindex(s)-3:end])
println(lastindex(s), " ", length(s))
s[1:4]
examples.output:
naïve
café
11 10
ERROR: StringIndexError: invalid index [4], valid nearby indices [3]=>'ï', [5]=>'v'
  @ top-level scope at line 5

sections.body:
A `for` loop over a string visits each **character**, decoding UTF-8 for you,
so it never hits an invalid index. `collect(s)` gives a `Vector{Char}`, and
functions such as `count`, `reverse` and `uppercase` work character by
character. Most of the time this is all you need, and you never touch byte
indices.

examples.code:
for c in "año"
    println(c, " ", typeof(c), " ", isletter(c))
end
println(collect("año"))
println(count(c -> c in "aeiou", "education"))
println(reverse("año"))
examples.output:
a Char true
ñ Char true
o Char true
['a', 'ñ', 'o']
5
oña

sections.body:
`parse(T, s)` reads a number of type `T` from a string and throws an
`ArgumentError` if the text is not one. When bad input is expected (user
input, messy files), use `tryparse`, which returns `nothing` instead of
throwing, and check for it with `=== nothing` or `isnothing`.

The reverse direction is `string(x)`.

examples.code:
println(parse(Int, "42") + 1)
println(parse(Float64, "2.5e3"))
println(tryparse(Int, "4x"))
println(isnothing(tryparse(Int, "4x")))
println(string(17) * "!")
parse(Int, "4x")

43
2500.0
nothing
true
17!
ERROR: ArgumentError: invalid base 10 digit 'x' in "4x"
  @ top-level scope at line 6

sections.title: Parsing numbers from text

sections.body:
`r"..."` is a regular expression (PCRE syntax). `match` returns the first
match or `nothing`; a match's capture groups are in `m.captures` (or `m[1]`,
`m[2]`, ...). `eachmatch` iterates over all matches.

Captures, like the pieces from `split`, are `SubString`s: views into the
original string, with no copy. They behave like strings; call `String(x)` when
you want an independent copy.

examples.code:
m = match(r"(\d+)-(\d+)", "pages 12-31 and 40-45")
println(m.match, " ", m[1], " ", m[2])
println([parse(Int, x.match) for x in eachmatch(r"\d+", "a1b22c333")])
println(match(r"z", "abc"))
println(typeof(m[1]))

words = split("the quick brown fox")
w = words[2]
println(typeof(w), " ", w, " ", length(w))
println(typeof(String(w)))

sections.body:
`if` ... `elseif` ... `else` ... `end` works as in most languages, and the
whole block is an expression with a value (unit 1). For a short choice
between two values, `cond ? a : b` (the *ternary* operator) is common; the
spaces around `?` and `:` are required.

A condition must be a `Bool`. Unlike Python, R or C, Julia does not treat `0`,
`""` or an empty array as false: `if 1` is an error. Write the comparison you
mean (`x != 0`, `!isempty(v)`).

examples.code:
x = -3
if x > 0
    println("positive")
elseif x == 0
    println("zero")
else
    println("negative")
end
println(iseven(x) ? "even" : "odd")

if 1
    println("never printed")
end

sections.body:
`a && b` evaluates `b` only when `a` is true; `a || b` evaluates `b` only
when `a` is false. Besides combining conditions, Julia code uses them as a
compact `if`: `cond && action` runs the action when `cond` holds, and
`cond || action` runs it when `cond` fails. Inside a function,
`x < 0 && return 0` is an idiomatic early exit.

Comparisons chain the way they do in mathematics: `1 < x < 3` means
`1 < x && x < 3`.

examples.code:
x = 7
x > 5 && println("x is bigger than 5")
x > 10 || println("x is not bigger than 10")
println(1 < x < 10, " ", 1 < x < 5, " ", 0 <= x == 7)
examples.output:
x is bigger than 5
x is not bigger than 10
true false true

examples.caption: The right-hand side is never evaluated when the left side decides the answer, so the division by zero does not happen.
`&&` as an early return inside a function.

sections.body:
`a:b` is the range from `a` to `b` **inclusive**, and `a:s:b` steps by `s`.
A range stores only its start, step and stop, not its elements; `collect`
turns it into a `Vector`. `length`, `step`, `reverse`, `first` and `last` all
work, and `5:1` is empty (count down with `5:-1:1`). `range(0, 1; length = 5)`
gives evenly spaced floats.

`for x in collection` loops over a range, a vector, a string, a tuple, and
more. `enumerate` gives index and value together, and `for i in 1:2, j in 1:3`
is a nested loop written on one line.

examples.code:
r = 1:2:9
println(collect(r), " length ", length(r), " step ", step(r))
println(collect(reverse(r)), " ", collect(10:-3:1))
println(isempty(5:1), " ", collect(range(0, 1; length = 5)))

for (i, fruit) in enumerate(["apple", "pear"])
    println(i, ": ", fruit)
end
for i in 1:2, j in 1:3
    print((i, j), " ")
end
println()

sections.body:
`while cond ... end` repeats while the condition holds. `break` leaves the
innermost loop, `continue` skips to its next iteration.

Julia has no labelled `break` for leaving several nested loops at once. The
idiomatic way is to put the search in a function and `return` from it as soon
as you have the answer, as `find_pair` does below.

examples.code:
p = 1
while p <= 1000
    p *= 2
end
println(p)
for i in 1:10
    iseven(i) && continue
    i > 7 && break
    print(i, " ")
end
println()

examples.caption: `return` leaves both loops at once.
examples.code:
function find_pair(v, target)
    for i in eachindex(v), j in i+1:lastindex(v)
        v[i] + v[j] == target && return (i, j)
    end
    return nothing
end
println(find_pair([3, 8, 1, 5], 6))
println(find_pair([3, 8, 1, 5], 100))

sections.body:
`for` and `while` loops (and functions) open a new *local scope*. A variable
first assigned inside the loop is local to it and does not exist afterwards.

The tricky case is a loop that updates a **global** variable, one defined at
the top level. In the REPL, and in this site's sandbox, such a loop
updates the global (the REPL's *soft scope*). In a file run with
`julia script.jl` or `include`, the same assignment inside the loop creates a
new *local* `total`, so `total += i` reads a local that has no value yet:
Julia prints a warning and then throws an `UndefVarError`.

Three fixes: write `global total += i` to say you mean the global, wrap the
code in a function (the usual answer: loops in functions are also much faster),
or use a `let` block. `local x` declares a fresh local explicitly.

examples.caption: REPL mode (the default here): the loop updates the global `total`.
examples.code:
total = 0
for i in 1:3
    total += i
end
total

examples.caption: The same code run as a file (`mode = "file"`): a warning, then an error.
examples.code:
total = 0
for i in 1:3
    total += i
end
total
examples.output:
┌ Warning: Assignment to `total` in soft scope is ambiguous because a global variable by the same name exists: `total` will be treated as a new local. Disambiguate by using `local total` to suppress this warning or `global total` to assign to the existing global variable.
└ @ main.jl:3
ERROR: UndefVarError: `total` not defined
  @ top-level scope at line 3

examples.caption: In a file: `global` fixes it, and so does putting the loop in a function.
examples.code:
total = 0
for i in 1:3
    global total += i
end
println(total)

function sum_to(n)
    t = 0
    for i in 1:n
        t += i
    end
    return t
end
println(sum_to(3))

examples.caption: A variable created inside a loop is gone after it, in any mode.
examples.code:
for i in 1:3
    sq = i^2
end
sq
examples.output:
ERROR: UndefVarError: `sq` not defined
  @ top level at line 4

examples.caption: `local` makes a new variable even when a global of the same name exists.
examples.code:
x = 10
for i in 1:2
    local x = i * 100
    println("inside: ", x)
end
println("outside: ", x)

sections.body:
The long form is `function name(args) ... end`; for a one-line body the short
form `name(args) = expression` is the same thing. A function returns the value
of its **last expression**, so `return` is only needed to leave early. A
function whose last expression is `println(...)` returns `nothing`.

To return several values, return a tuple; the caller can *destructure* it
into separate variables. `_` throws a value away.

examples.code:
function hypot2(a, b)
    s = a^2 + b^2
    sqrt(s)            # last expression: the return value
end
area(r) = π * r^2      # short form
sign_word(x) = x < 0 ? "negative" : "non-negative"
println(hypot2(3, 4), " ", area(1.0), " ", sign_word(-2))

function stats(v)
    return minimum(v), maximum(v), sum(v) / length(v)
end
lo, hi, avg = stats([4, 8, 1, 7])
println("lo = $lo, hi = $hi, avg = $avg")
_, top, _ = stats([4, 8, 1, 7])
println(top)
stats([1, 2])

sections.body:
Positional arguments can have defaults: `f(x, n = 2)`. Arguments after a
semicolon are **keyword arguments**, passed by name in any order
(`round_to(x; digits = 2)`); they are best for options. A keyword argument
cannot be passed by position, as the error shows.

`args...` in a definition collects any number of arguments into a tuple
(*varargs*). In a call, `f(v...)` does the opposite: it *splats* a collection
into separate arguments.

sections.title: Default, keyword and variable arguments

sections.body:
`x -> x^2` is a function without a name (`(a, b) -> a + b` for two
arguments). Functions are values, so you can pass them to other functions:
`map(f, v)` applies `f` to each element, `filter(pred, v)` keeps the elements
for which `pred` is `true`, and `sort(v; by = f)` sorts by the key `f(x)`.

When the function argument is long, a **do-block** passes it as the first
argument: `map(v) do x ... end` is `map(x -> ..., v)`.

examples.code:
v = [3, -1, 4, -1, 5]
println(map(x -> x^2, v))
println(filter(x -> x > 0, v))
words = ["pear", "fig", "banana", "kiwi"]
println(sort(words; by = length))
println(sort(words; by = w -> (length(w), w), rev = true))

labels = map([7, 12, 15]) do n
    if n % 15 == 0
        "fifteen-ish"
    elseif n % 2 == 0
        "even"
    else
        "odd"
    end
end
println(labels)
sum(1:4) do x
    x^2
end

sections.title: Anonymous functions, map, filter, sort and do-blocks

sections.body:
A function defined inside another function can use the outer function's
local variables; it *closes over* them, so it is called a **closure**.
`make_adder(n)` returns a new function that remembers its own `n`.

A closure captures the *variable*, not a snapshot of its value, so it can
update it, like the counter below. In a loop, each iteration has a fresh
loop variable, so closures made in a comprehension each see their own `i`
(Python programmers expect `[3, 3, 3]` here).

examples.code:
make_adder(n) = x -> x + n
add5 = make_adder(5)
add10 = make_adder(10)
println(add5(1), " ", add10(1))

function make_counter()
    count = 0
    return () -> (count += 1)
end
c = make_counter()
c(); c()
println(c())
fs = [() -> i for i in 1:3]
[f() for f in fs]

sections.title: Closures capture variables

sections.body:
By convention a function whose name ends in `!` **modifies one of its
arguments** (usually the first): `sort!(v)` sorts `v` in place, while `sort(v)`
returns a sorted copy and leaves `v` alone. `push!`, `append!` and `fill!`
follow the same rule. The `!` is only part of the name; Julia does not
enforce it, but every Julia programmer reads it as a warning, so follow it in
your own code.

Function arguments without type annotations accept anything that supports the
operations used. One definition of `f(x) = 2x + 1` works for an `Int`, a
`Float64`, a `Rational` and a `BigInt`, and Julia compiles a specialised
version for each type, so generic code is not slow.

examples.code:
v = [3, 1, 2]
w = sort(v)
println(v, " ", w)
sort!(v)
println(v)

function double!(v)
    for i in eachindex(v)
        v[i] *= 2
    end
    return v
end
double!(v)
println(v)

sections.body:
A `Vector` is written with square brackets and commas. Every array has an
**element type**, shown by `eltype` and in the type itself: `[1, 2, 3]` is a
`Vector{Int64}`. Mixing integers and floats promotes them to a common type, so
`[1, 2.5]` is a `Vector{Float64}`.

An empty `[]` has nothing to infer from, so it is a `Vector{Any}`, which can
hold anything and is slow to compute with. When you start empty and fill a
vector later, give the element type: `Int[]` or `Float64[]`.

Indexing is **1-based**, as in MATLAB, R and Fortran, and unlike Python or C:
`v[1]` is the first element and `v[end]` the last. `v[0]` is an error.

examples.code:

println(v[1], " ", v[end], " ", v[end-1], " length ", length(v))
println(typeof([1, 2.5]), " ", typeof(Int[]), " ", typeof([]))

sections.body:
`v[2:3]` makes a **new array** holding copies of those elements: changing
the slice does not change `v`. This differs from NumPy, where a basic slice is
a view. When you want a window into the original without copying, use
`view(v, 2:3)` or the `@view` macro; the performance unit comes back to views.

Assignment never copies. After `b = a`, the two names refer to the *same*
array, so a change through `b` is visible through `a` (`===` tells you they
are the same object). `copy(a)` makes a new outer array; for an array of
arrays the inner arrays are still shared, and `deepcopy` copies all the way
down.

examples.code:
a = [1, 2, 3, 4]
s = a[2:3]        # a copy
s[1] = 100
v = view(a, 2:3)  # a window into a
v[2] = -1
println(s)
println(a)

examples.caption: `b = a` gives the same array a second name; `copy` makes a new one.
examples.code:

b = a
c = copy(a)
b[1] = 99
println(a, " ", c)
println(a === b, " ", a === c)

sections.body:
Inside brackets, spaces separate columns and `;` (or a new line) separates
rows, so `[1 2 3; 4 5 6]` is a 2×3 `Matrix{Int64}`. Index with `A[row, col]`;
`size(A)` is `(rows, columns)`.

Julia stores a matrix **column by column** (like Fortran and MATLAB, unlike
C and NumPy's default). `vec(A)` shows that memory order: down the first
column, then the second. `reshape` reuses the same order, so `reshape(1:6, 2, 3)`
fills columns first (reshaping a range gives a lazy wrapper rather than a new
`Matrix`; `collect` it if you need one). Loops over a matrix are fastest when the *first* index
changes fastest.

examples.code:
A = [1 2 3; 4 5 6]
println(size(A), " ", A[2, 1], " ", A[1, end])
println(vec(A))
reshape(1:6, 2, 3)

examples.caption: A column `A[:, j]` is contiguous in memory; a row is not. Both are copies here.

println(A[1, :])

sections.title: Matrices are column-major

sections.body:
A `Tuple` is a fixed-length, **immutable** sequence written with parentheses:
`(1, "a", 2.5)`. Each position keeps its own type, which is why functions
return several values as a tuple and why tuples are cheap: no heap array is
created. You can index a tuple and destructure it, but not change it.

A `NamedTuple` adds a name to each position, `(x = 1, y = 2)`, read with
`p.x`. It is a lightweight record when a full struct (see the types unit)
would be overkill.

examples.code:
t = (1, "a", 2.5)
println(typeof(t), " ", t[2])
n, s, f = t           # destructuring
p = (x = 1, y = 2.5)
println(p.x + p.y, " ", keys(p), " ", typeof(p))
t[1] = 5

Tuple{Int64, String, Float64} a
3.5 (:x, :y) @NamedTuple{x::Int64, y::Float64}
ERROR: MethodError: no method matching setindex!(::Tuple{Int64, String, Float64}, ::Int64, ::Int64)
  @ top-level scope at line 6

sections.title: Tuples and named tuples

sections.body:
A `Dict` maps keys to values. Build one from `key => value` pairs; read with
`d[key]` (an error if the key is absent) or `get(d, key, default)`; test with
`haskey`. Assigning `d[key] = value` adds or replaces. Iterating a `Dict`
gives `key => value` pairs, which you can destructure in the `for`. The order
is determined by hashing, not insertion, so sort the keys when the order
matters.

A `Set` holds each value at most once. `in` (also written `∈`, `\in` Tab)
asks whether a value is present; `union` and `intersect` combine sets.

examples.code:
ages = Dict("ada" => 36, "alan" => 41)
ages["grace"] = 85
println(ages["ada"], " ", get(ages, "linus", 0), " ", haskey(ages, "alan"))
for (name, age) in sort(collect(ages))
    println(name, " is ", age)
end
println(sort(collect(keys(ages))), " ", sum(values(ages)))
examples.output:
36 0 true
ada is 36
alan is 41
grace is 85
["ada", "alan", "grace"] 162

examples.code:
a = Set([1, 2, 3, 3, 3])
b = Set([2, 3, 4])
println(length(a), " ", 2 in a, " ", 5 ∈ a)
println(sort(collect(union(a, b))), " ", sort(collect(intersect(a, b))))

examples.caption: `x in v` scans a Vector element by element; a Set looks the value up by its hash. (Timing-based, so not compared between runs.)
examples.code:

s = Set(v)
lookups(c) = count(x -> x in c, 100_001:100_200)   # 200 absent values
lookups(v); lookups(s)                              # compile first
t_vec = @elapsed lookups(v)
t_set = @elapsed lookups(s)
println("Set at least 50x faster: ", t_vec > 50 * t_set)

sections.body:
A comprehension builds an array from a loop in one expression:
`[f(x) for x in xs]`, optionally filtered with `if`. Two `for` clauses
separated by a comma build a **matrix**, the first variable running down the
rows.

`sort(v)` returns a new sorted array; `sort!(v)` sorts `v` in place. Both
accept `rev = true` and `by = f` (sort by `f(x)`). `sortperm(v)` returns the
*indices* that would sort `v`, which lets you reorder a second array the same
way.

examples.code:

[i * j for i in 1:3, j in 1:4]

scores = [72, 95, 88]
println(sort(scores), " ", sort(names, by = length), " ", sort(scores, rev = true))
p = sortperm(scores, rev = true)
println(p, " ", names[p])
sort!(names)
names

sections.body:
In Julia, `f.(x)` calls `f` on every element of `x` and collects the results.
This works for **every** function, including your own; there is no separate
list of "vectorized" functions as in NumPy or R. Operators get the dot in
front: `.+`, `.*`, `.^`, `.<`.

Without the dot, an operator means its mathematical meaning. `v * 2` is fine
(scaling a vector), but `v + 1` is an error, because adding a number to a

sections.title: The dot: any function, elementwise

sections.body:
When several dotted calls are nested, Julia **fuses** them into a single loop
over the elements and allocates only the final result. `sin.(x) .+ 2 .* x .^ 2`
does not build `sin.(x)`, then `x .^ 2`, then `2 .* (...)`: it computes the
whole expression for one element at a time.

Writing the same thing in steps creates a temporary array at every step. The
example measures the bytes each version allocates, in units of the size of
`x`: the fused version allocates one array's worth, the stepwise one four.

examples.code:
fused(x) = sin.(x) .+ 2 .* x .^ 2
function stepwise(x)
    a = sin.(x)
    b = x .^ 2
    c = 2 .* b
    return a .+ c
end
x = rand(1000)
fused(x); stepwise(x)        # compile first
println(fused(x) == stepwise(x))
println("allocated, in sizes of x: fused ", round(@allocated(fused(x)) / sizeof(x), digits = 1),
        ", stepwise ", round(@allocated(stepwise(x)) / sizeof(x), digits = 1))
examples.output:
true
allocated, in sizes of x: fused 1.0, stepwise 4.1

sections.title: Fusion: one loop, no temporaries

sections.body:
`y = x .* 2` creates a new array and binds the name `y` to it. `y .= x .* 2`
instead **writes into** the array `y` already refers to, so the fused loop
allocates nothing at all. This is how you update arrays inside a loop without
creating garbage.

Dots everywhere get noisy; the `@.` macro adds a dot to every call and
operator in an expression, including the assignment: `@. y = 2x^2 + 1` is
`y .= 2 .* x .^ 2 .+ 1`.

examples.code:
x = [1.0, 2.0, 3.0]
y = zeros(3)
z = y            # a second name for the same array
y .= x .* 2      # writes into it: z sees the change
println(z)
y = x .* 10      # a new array; z still holds the old one
println(y, " ", z)

examples.caption: `@.` dots everything; an in-place update inside a function allocates 0 bytes.
examples.code:
function update!(y, x)
    @. y = 2x^2 + 1
    return y
end
x = collect(1.0:4.0)
y = similar(x)
update!(y, x)
println(y)
println(@allocated update!(y, x))

sections.body:
Broadcasting is more than "same-length arrays". Dimensions of length 1 are
**stretched** to match: a column vector (a `Vector`, n×1) combined with a row
(a 1×m matrix such as `[10 20]` or `v'`) gives an n×m matrix, without writing
a loop. A scalar is stretched along every dimension. Shapes that cannot be
matched give a `DimensionMismatch`.

To treat a whole container as a single value inside a broadcast, wrap it in
`Ref(...)` (or a one-element tuple).

examples.code:
col = [1, 2, 3]
row = [10 20]
println(size(col), " ", size(row))
col .+ row

sections.title: Broadcasting shapes

sections.body:
Functions are values, so many functions take one as their first argument.
`map(f, xs)` is like `f.(xs)`; `filter(pred, xs)` keeps the elements where
`pred` is true; `reduce(op, xs)` combines them with a binary operator;
`mapreduce(f, op, xs)` does both in one pass without an intermediate array.
`foldl` and `foldr` fix the order of combination, which matters for
operators like `-`.

The everyday reductions also accept a function first: `sum(abs2, v)`,
`maximum(length, words)`, `count(iseven, v)`, `any(>(3), v)`, `all(...)`.
These do not build `f.(v)` first. `>(3)` is a function that tests `x > 3`.

examples.code:
v = [3, -1, 4, -1, 5]
println(map(x -> 2x, v), " ", filter(>(0), v))
println(reduce(+, v), " ", mapreduce(abs, +, v), " ", foldl(-, 1:4), " ", foldr(-, 1:4))
println(sum(abs2, v), " ", count(iseven, v), " ", any(>(4), v), " ", all(>(0), v))
println(maximum(length, ["a", "abc", "ab"]))

sections.title: map, filter, reduce and functions as arguments

sections.body:
Unlike in Python or R, a plain `for` loop in Julia compiles to fast machine
code, so you never need to contort an algorithm into array operations for
speed. Broadcasting is for *expressing* elementwise work concisely. Write a
loop when the work is sequential (each step depends on the last), when you can
stop early, or when a chain of array operations would allocate several
temporaries.

The loop below stops at the first point where a running total passes a
threshold, something that is awkward to say with whole-array operations.

examples.code:
function first_crossing(v, limit)
    total = zero(eltype(v))
    for (i, x) in enumerate(v)
        total += x
        total > limit && return i
    end
    return nothing
end
println(first_crossing([3, 1, 4, 1, 5, 9], 8))
println(first_crossing([1, 1], 8))

sections.body:
`typeof(x)` is the type of a value; `x isa T` asks whether it belongs to `T`
(or to a subtype of `T`). Types form a single tree with `Any` at the top:
`supertype` walks up, `subtypes` lists the children (it lives in the
`InteractiveUtils` standard library, which the REPL loads for you; here we
load it explicitly).

**Abstract** types such as `Real` and `Integer` only group other types; no
value has an abstract type as its `typeof`. **Concrete** types such as
`Int64` and `Float64` are the leaves that values actually have. The lists
below are those of Julia 1.10 with only Base loaded; packages can add more
subtypes.

examples.code:

println(typeof(1), " ", 1 isa Integer, " ", 1 isa AbstractFloat, " ", 1.0 isa Real)
println(supertype(Int64), " → ", supertype(Signed), " → ", supertype(Integer), " → ", supertype(Real))
println(subtypes(Real))
println(subtypes(Integer))
println(isconcretetype(Int64), " ", isabstracttype(Integer), " ", isconcretetype(Real))

sections.title: Every value has a type, in one tree

sections.body:
`struct` defines a new concrete type with named fields. Its values are
**immutable**: once created, a field cannot be reassigned. That lets the
compiler store them inline in arrays and registers, much like a tuple with
names. When you need to change a field, use `mutable struct`; those values
live on the heap and are shared by reference, like arrays.

Julia defines a default constructor that takes the fields in order and
converts each argument to the field's declared type (so `Point(1, 2)` stores
`1.0` and `2.0`). In the REPL you cannot redefine a struct with different
fields; restart Julia (or use a new name) when you change one.

examples.code:
struct Point
    x::Float64
    y::Float64
end
p = Point(1, 2)
println(p, " ", p.x + p.y, " ", fieldnames(Point))
p.x = 5
examples.output:

ERROR: setfield!: immutable struct of type Point cannot be changed

sections.body:
An **inner constructor** is a function inside the `struct` block that calls
`new(...)`. Once you write one, the default constructor is gone, so every
value of the type has passed your checks: here, an `Interval` with `lo > hi`
cannot exist. Throw an `ArgumentError` for a bad argument.

An **outer constructor** is an ordinary method defined outside the block,
usually a convenience that calls another constructor.

`Base.@kwdef` lets a struct have default values and keyword construction,
which suits configuration records.

examples.code:
struct Interval
    lo::Float64
    hi::Float64
    function Interval(lo, hi)
        lo <= hi || throw(ArgumentError("need lo <= hi, got $lo > $hi"))
        return new(lo, hi)
    end
end
Interval(x) = Interval(x, x)       # outer constructor: a single point
println(Interval(1, 3), " ", Interval(2))
Interval(3, 1)

sections.body:
A field declared with an abstract type, such as `x::Real`, can hold any
`Real`, so the compiler cannot know what reading it returns: every use is a
run-time type check and the value is stored boxed. A field with no type at all
is `Any`, the worst case.

A **parametric** type keeps the flexibility without the cost: `Point2{T}` has
fields of type `T`, and `Point2(1, 2)` is a `Point2{Int64}`, a concrete type.
`Base.return_types` shows what the compiler infers for a function on given
argument types: `Real`-field reads infer `Any`, parametric ones `Float64`.
Both fields share one `T`, so mixing `1` and `2.5` has no matching
constructor unless you add one (the dispatch unit shows how, with `promote`).
The performance unit returns to this; the `L02` lesson drills it.

    y::T

sections.body:
`Union{A, B}` is the type of values that are either an `A` or a `B`. Two
special values are common partners in a Union:

* `nothing` (type `Nothing`) means "no value": `findfirst` returns it when
  nothing is found. It is not a number; arithmetic on it is an error. Test
  with `x === nothing` or `isnothing(x)`.
* `missing` (type `Missing`) means "a value exists but is unknown", as in
  statistics and SQL's `NULL`. It **propagates**: `missing + 1` is `missing`,
  and so is `missing == 1`. Use `ismissing(x)` to test, `skipmissing(v)` to
  iterate over the known values, and `coalesce(x, default)` to replace it.

`isequal` treats `missing` as equal to itself, which is why dictionaries and
the grader use it.

println(typeof(v), " ", sum(v), " ", sum(skipmissing(v)), " ", coalesce.(v, 0))
println(missing + 1, " ", missing == 1, " ", missing == missing, " ", isequal(missing, missing))

Each definition `f(args) = ...` with a different signature adds a
**method** to the same generic function `f`; it does not replace the previous
one. `methods(f)` lists them. When you call `f`, Julia picks the most specific
method that matches the types of the arguments **at run time**. The order in
which the methods were defined plays no part.

A method with no annotation on an argument accepts `Any`. Methods can also
differ in the number of arguments.

describe(x) = "something"
describe(x::Real) = "a real number"
describe(x::Integer) = "an integer"
describe(x, y) = "two things"
println(describe("hi"), ", ", describe(2.5), ", ", describe(3), ", ", describe(1, 2))
methods(describe)

sections.body:
Julia looks at **every** argument, not just the first (a method does not
belong to the class of its first argument, as in Python or Java). Among the
methods that match, the one whose signature is a subtype of all the others
wins. In the example, `(Int, Number)` beats `(Number, Number)` for `(1, 2.0)`,
and `(Number, Int)` beats it for `(2.0, 1)`.

The types are those of the *values*: a `Vector{Any}` holding `3` still
dispatches on `Int64`.

examples.code:
combine(x::Number, y::Number) = "numbers"

combine(x::Number, y::Int) = "int second"
println(combine(1.0, 2.0), " | ", combine(1, 2.0), " | ", combine(2.0, 1))
items = Any[3, 2.5]
println(combine(items[1], items[2]))

sections.body:
Code like `if s isa Circle ... elseif s isa Rect ... end` has to be edited
every time someone adds a shape. With dispatch each type brings its own
method, and code written against the abstract type (`sum(area, shapes)`) works
for shapes that did not exist when it was written. A new type only needs new
methods; nothing else changes.

examples.code:
abstract type Shape end
struct Circle <: Shape
    r::Float64
end
struct Rect <: Shape
    w::Float64
    h::Float64
end
area(c::Circle) = π * c.r^2
area(r::Rect) = r.w * r.h

shapes = Shape[Circle(1), Rect(2, 3)]
println(round(sum(area, shapes), digits = 4))

struct Square <: Shape        # added later, nothing else edited
    s::Float64
end
area(q::Square) = q.s^2
push!(shapes, Square(2))
println(round(sum(area, shapes), digits = 4))

sections.title: Methods instead of isa chains

sections.body:
Base functions are generic functions too, so you add methods to them for your
own types: `Base.show(io::IO, p::Point)` decides how a value prints (in
arrays, in `println`, everywhere), and `Base.:+` lets `+`, and therefore
`sum`, work on your type. Only add methods where at least one argument is
your own type; adding `Base.:+(::Int, ::String)` would change behaviour for
everyone ("type piracy").

Equality comes as a set. If you define `==`, define `hash` consistently
(equal values must have equal hashes), because `Dict` and `Set` use `isequal`
together with `hash`; `isequal` falls back to `==`. The default `==` on a
struct compares fields with `===`, which for a `Vector` field means "the same
array", not "equal contents". In the example the Set still has two elements
after `==` is defined, until `hash` is defined to match.

examples.code:
struct Point
    x::Float64
    y::Float64
end
Base.show(io::IO, p::Point) = print(io, "(", p.x, ", ", p.y, ")")
Base.:+(a::Point, b::Point) = Point(a.x + b.x, a.y + b.y)
pts = [Point(1, 2), Point(3, 4), Point(0.5, 0)]
println(Point(1, 2) + Point(3, 4))
println(sum(pts))
pts

struct Bag
    items::Vector{Int}
end
println(Bag([1]) == Bag([1]), " ", length(Set([Bag([1]), Bag([1])])))
Base.:(==)(a::Bag, b::Bag) = a.items == b.items
println(Bag([1]) == Bag([1]), " ", length(Set([Bag([1]), Bag([1])])))
Base.hash(b::Bag, h::UInt) = hash(b.items, hash(:Bag, h))
println(length(Set([Bag([1]), Bag([1])])))

sections.title: Extending Base for your types

sections.body:
How does `1 + 2.5` work without a method for every pair of number types?
Base has a fallback `+(x::Number, y::Number) = +(promote(x, y)...)`:
`promote` converts its arguments to a common type, chosen by
`promote_type`, and then the same-type method runs. `convert(T, x)` converts
one value, and refuses when the value would change (`InexactError`).

The same trick fixes the `Point2(1, 2.5)` error from the types unit: an outer

sections.body:
When a function cannot do what it was asked, it **throws** an exception:
`throw(x)` stops the function and unwinds the call stack until something
catches `x`. If nothing does, the program stops and prints the error.

An exception is an ordinary value whose type is a subtype of `Exception`.
`throw(DomainError(x, "message"))` says "this argument is outside the
function's domain"; `error("message")` is a shortcut that throws an
`ErrorException` with that message. Prefer a specific type when one fits:
code that catches errors can tell a `DomainError` from an `ArgumentError`,
but every `error(...)` looks the same.

Notice in the output that the message names the type, then the value, then
your text, and the `@` line points at the line of your code where the failing
call was made.

checked_sqrt needs a non-negative number

sections.body:
Base Julia throws a handful of exception types over and over. Learning them
makes error messages quick to read:

* `DomainError`: the argument has the right type but a bad value (`sqrt(-1.0)`).
* `ArgumentError`: an argument is invalid in some other way (`parse(Int, "12a")`).
* `BoundsError`: an index is outside the array (Julia never wraps around or
  silently extends, unlike negative indices in Python).
* `KeyError`: a `Dict` has no such key.
* `MethodError`: no method of the function accepts these argument types.

The hierarchy is flat: each of these is a direct subtype of `Exception`, so
`catch` can tell them apart by type but there is no "LookupError" family to
catch at once, as Python has.

examples.caption: Each call fails with a different type; we print the type and the first line of the message.
examples.code:
attempts = [
    () -> sqrt(-1.0),
    () -> parse(Int, "12a"),
    () -> [10, 20, 30][4],
    () -> Dict("a" => 1)["b"],
    () -> "abc" + 1,
]
for f in attempts
    try
        f()
    catch e
        msg = first(split(sprint(showerror, e), '\n'))
        println(rpad(string(typeof(e)), 15), first(msg, 70))
    end
end
examples.output:
DomainError    DomainError with -1.0:
ArgumentError  ArgumentError: invalid base 10 digit 'a' in "12a"
BoundsError    BoundsError: attempt to access 3-element Vector{Int64} at index [4]
KeyError       KeyError: key "b" not found
MethodError    MethodError: no method matching +(::String, ::Int64)

DomainError <: Exception
ArgumentError <: Exception
BoundsError <: Exception
KeyError <: Exception
MethodError <: Exception
ErrorException <: Exception

sections.body:
`try ... catch e ... end` runs the `try` block, and if anything in it throws,
runs the `catch` block with the exception bound to `e`. Two optional parts
complete the picture:

* `else` (Julia 1.8 and later) runs only when the `try` block did **not** throw.
  Code there is not protected by the `catch`, which keeps the `try` block small.
* `finally` runs **always**: after a normal finish, after a caught error, and
  even when the error propagates out. It is where cleanup goes.

Each block has its own scope, so a variable assigned only inside `try` is not
visible in `else`; declare it first with `local n`, as below.

`catch e` catches *everything*, including typos (`UndefVarError`) and bugs.
To handle one kind of failure only, test the type and rethrow the rest:
`e isa KeyError || rethrow()`. `rethrow()` re-throws the current exception
with its original backtrace.

examples.code:
function describe(s)
    local n
    try
        n = parse(Int, s)
    catch e
        println("  cannot parse ", repr(s), ": ", typeof(e))
    else
        println("  parsed ", repr(s), " as ", n)
    finally
        println("  finished ", repr(s))
    end
end
describe("12")
describe("twelve")
examples.output:
parsed "12" as 12
  finished "12"
  cannot parse "twelve": ArgumentError
  finished "twelve"

    try
        return container[key]
    catch e
        e isa KeyError || rethrow()
        return "missing"
    end
end
d = Dict("a" => 1)
println(lookup(d, "a"))
println(lookup(d, "z"))
lookup([10, 20], "a")

missing
ERROR: ArgumentError: invalid index: "a" of type String

sections.title: try, catch, else, finally

sections.body:
An exception type is a `struct` that subtypes `Exception`. Fields carry the
details, and a method of `Base.showerror(io, e)` controls the message that
`showerror` (and the REPL, for an uncaught error) prints. Callers can then
catch exactly your error with `e isa ValidationError` and leave every other
error alone.

`@assert cond "message"` throws an `AssertionError` when `cond` is false. Use
it for **invariants**: things that can only be false if *your* code has a bug.
Do not use it to validate user input: the manual warns that assertions may be
disabled at some optimization levels, and an `AssertionError` tells the
caller nothing about what they passed. Throw `ArgumentError` or `DomainError`
for bad input instead.

examples.code:
struct ValidationError <: Exception
    field::String
    reason::String
end
Base.showerror(io::IO, e::ValidationError) =
    print(io, "ValidationError: ", e.field, " ", e.reason)

function check_user(name, age)
    isempty(name) && throw(ValidationError("name", "must not be empty"))
    age >= 0 || throw(ValidationError("age", "must be non-negative, got $age"))
    return (name, age)
end
println(check_user("Ada", 36))
try
    check_user("Bob", -1)
catch e
    e isa ValidationError || rethrow()
    showerror(stdout, e)
    println()
    println("the bad field was ", e.field)
end
examples.output:
("Ada", 36)
ValidationError: age must be non-negative, got -1
the bad field was age

sections.body:
Not every failure is exceptional. When "not found" or "not a number" is a
normal outcome, Base returns `nothing` instead of throwing:

* `tryparse(Int, s)` returns the number or `nothing` (`parse` throws).
* `findfirst(pred, v)` returns an index or `nothing`.
* `get(d, key, default)` returns `default` for a missing key (`d[key]` throws).

The caller checks with `=== nothing` (or `isnothing`), or supplies a default
with `something(x, default)`. Prefer this style in hot loops: throwing and
catching an exception costs far more than returning a value (the
`parse-ints-count-failures` problem below lets the grader measure it).

examples.code:
println(tryparse(Int, "42"))
println(tryparse(Int, "4x2"))
println(findfirst(==(7), [3, 5, 7, 9]))
println(findfirst(==(8), [3, 5, 7, 9]))
println(get(Dict("a" => 1), "b", 0))
println(something(tryparse(Int, "oops"), -1))
x = tryparse(Float64, "2.5e3")
x === nothing ? "not a number" : 2x

sections.title: Returning nothing instead of throwing

sections.body:
To process many items and keep going past bad ones, put the `try` inside the
loop and collect what failed. Catch only the error you expect, so a real bug
still stops the program.

Resources (files, locks, connections) must be released even when the work
fails. The pattern is a function that takes the work as its first argument
and wraps it in `try ... finally`. Julia's `do` block syntax passes the block
as that first argument: `with_resource(name) do r ... end` is
`with_resource(r -> ..., name)`. Notice that `close db` is printed *before*
the error: `finally` ran on the way out. `open(path) do io ... end` (the I/O
unit) works exactly this way and closes the file for you.

examples.code:
inputs = ["1", "2", "three", "4", ""]
total = 0
bad = String[]
for s in inputs
    try
        total += parse(Int, s)
    catch e
        e isa ArgumentError || rethrow()
        push!(bad, s)
    end
end
println("total = ", total, ", rejected: ", bad)

function with_resource(f, name)
    println("open ", name)
    try
        return f(name)
    finally
        println("close ", name)
    end
end
r = with_resource("cache") do res
    "used $res"
end
println(r)
with_resource("db") do res
    println("querying ", res)
    error("query failed")
end
examples.output:

close cache
used cache
open db
querying db
close db
ERROR: query failed

  @ with_resource at line 4
  @ top-level scope at line 13

sections.body:
Anything you can loop over implements one function, `iterate`:

* `iterate(x)` returns `(first_item, state)`, or `nothing` if `x` is empty;
* `iterate(x, state)` returns `(next_item, next_state)`, or `nothing` when done.

The state is whatever the type finds convenient: for a `Vector` it is the
next index, for a `String` the byte index of the next character. A loop
`for c in s ... end` is rewritten by the compiler into exactly the `while`
loop below, so arrays, strings, ranges, dictionaries and your own types all
work the same way.

In the second example notice that the state jumps from 2 to 4: `é` takes two
bytes in UTF-8, so string states are byte positions, not character counts.

examples.caption: What `for c in "hé!"` lowers to.
examples.code:
s = "hé!"
next = iterate(s)
while next !== nothing
    (c, state) = next
    println(c, "   next state = ", state)
    next = iterate(s, state)
end
examples.output:
h   next state = 2
é   next state = 4
!   next state = 5

sections.title: The iteration protocol

sections.body:
To make a type iterable, add methods to `Base.iterate` (one-argument and
two-argument; a default value for the state gives both at once). Two more
methods let the rest of Julia use your iterator well:

* `Base.length(x)` if you know the number of items; `collect` uses it to
  allocate the result once. If you do not know it, declare
  `Base.IteratorSize(::Type{T}) = Base.SizeUnknown()` (or `IsInfinite()`);
  the default is `HasLength()`, which promises a `length` method.
* `Base.eltype(::Type{T})`, so `collect` builds a `Vector{Int}` and not a
  vector with an element type guessed from the items.

Once `iterate` exists you get `for`, `collect`, `sum`, `maximum`, `in`,
`enumerate` and the whole `Iterators` module for free.

examples.code:
struct Countdown
    from::Int
end
Base.iterate(c::Countdown, n = c.from) = n < 1 ? nothing : (n, n - 1)
Base.length(c::Countdown) = c.from
Base.eltype(::Type{Countdown}) = Int

for k in Countdown(3)
    print(k, " ")
end
println()
println(collect(Countdown(5)))
println(sum(Countdown(100)), "  ", 2 in Countdown(3), "  ", maximum(Countdown(4)))

    n == 0 ? nothing : (n, n == 1 ? 0 : iseven(n) ? n ÷ 2 : 3n + 1)

for n in Collatz(6)
    print(n, " ")
end
println()
collect(Collatz(6))

sections.body:
`[f(x) for x in xs]` is a **comprehension**: it computes every value now and
stores them in a new array. `(f(x) for x in xs)` (round brackets, or no
brackets as the only argument of a function: `sum(f(x) for x in xs)`) is a
**generator**: an iterator that computes each value when asked for it and
stores nothing.

Use a generator when the values are consumed once, by `sum`, `maximum`,
`any`, a loop: it allocates no array. Use a comprehension when you need the
values again, or need to index them. Notice in the second example that
nothing is printed until `first` pulls one value out, and only one value is
computed.

examples.caption: Inside functions, the generator version allocates nothing; the comprehension allocates a 1000-element array.
examples.code:
sum_sq_eager(v) = sum([x^2 for x in v])
sum_sq_lazy(v) = sum(x^2 for x in v)
bytes(f, v) = (f(v); @allocated f(v))

v = collect(1:1000)
println(sum_sq_eager(v) == sum_sq_lazy(v))
println("eager: ", bytes(sum_sq_eager, v) >= 8000, "   lazy: ", bytes(sum_sq_lazy, v), " bytes")

g = (begin println("computing ", i); i^2 end for i in 1:3)
println("nothing computed yet")
first(g)

sections.title: Generators are lazy, comprehensions are eager

sections.body:
A few wrappers turn up in almost every loop:

* `enumerate(xs)` yields `(i, x)` pairs, counting from 1;
* `zip(a, b)` walks two collections in step and **stops at the shorter one**;
* `pairs(v)` yields `index => value` (for a `Dict`, `key => value`);
* `eachindex(v)` gives the valid indices of `v`; prefer it to `1:length(v)`,
  which assumes indices start at 1.

The `Iterators` module adds lazy versions of the usual list operations:
`Iterators.take(it, n)`, `Iterators.drop(it, n)`, `Iterators.filter(pred, it)`,
`Iterators.map(f, it)`, plus `Iterators.product` (all combinations),
`Iterators.partition` (chunks of a fixed size), `Iterators.flatten` (one
level of nesting removed) and `Iterators.countfrom` (1, 2, 3, ... forever).
Nothing is computed until something like `collect`, `sum` or a loop consumes
the result.

examples.code:
names = ["ada", "bob", "cy"]
ages = [36, 41, 29]
for (i, name) in enumerate(names)
    println(i, ": ", name)
end
for (name, age) in zip(names, ages)
    println(name, " is ", age)
end
println(collect(zip(1:10, "ab")))
println(collect(pairs(["x", "y"])))
println(eachindex(ages))
examples.output:
1: ada
2: bob
3: cy
ada is 36
bob is 41
cy is 29
[(1, 'a'), (2, 'b')]
[1 => "x", 2 => "y"]
Base.OneTo(3)

println(collect(Iterators.partition(1:7, 3)))
println(collect(Iterators.flatten([[1, 2], [3], Int[], [4]])))
println(collect(Iterators.drop("hello", 2)))

sections.body:
`Iterators.countfrom`, `Iterators.cycle` and `Iterators.repeated` never end.
They are useful as long as something stops them: `take` (a fixed count),
`takewhile` (until a condition fails), `first` of a filtered iterator (the
first match),
or a `break` in a loop.

Collecting an infinite iterator is refused: `IteratorSize` reports
`IsInfinite()` and `collect` has no method for it, so you get a
`MethodError` straight away instead of a program that never finishes.

examples.code:
println(collect(Iterators.take(Iterators.cycle([:red, :green]), 5)))
println(collect(Iterators.takewhile(<(100), (2^k for k in Iterators.countfrom(0)))))
println(first(Iterators.dropwhile(x -> x^2 < 50, Iterators.countfrom(1))))
println(first(Iterators.filter(x -> x^2 > 50, Iterators.countfrom(1))))

println(Base.IteratorSize(Iterators.countfrom(1)))
collect(Iterators.countfrom(1))

`module Name ... end` creates a separate global namespace: names defined
inside do not collide with names outside. From outside, refer to them with a
**qualified name**, `Geometry.perimeter`. Module names are capitalized by
convention.

`export area` marks `area` as part of the module's public interface;
`using .Geometry` then makes the exported names available unqualified (and
the module name itself). Unexported names stay reachable with a qualified
name. The leading dot in `.Geometry` means "the module defined right here",
as opposed to an installed package (`using Statistics`).

Unlike Python, a module is not tied to a file: one file can define several
modules, and one module is usually spread over several files.

examples.code:
module Geometry
export area
const UNIT = "m²"
area(w, h) = w * h
perimeter(w, h) = 2(w + h)
end

using .Geometry
println(area(2, 3), " ", Geometry.UNIT)
println(Geometry.perimeter(2, 3))
println(names(Geometry))
perimeter(2, 3)
examples.output:
6 m²
10
[:Geometry, :area]
ERROR: UndefVarError: `perimeter` not defined
  @ top-level scope at line 12

sections.title: A module is a namespace

sections.body:
The forms you will see:

* `using .M` brings in `M` and every name `M` exports.
* `using .M: f, g` brings in only `f` and `g`.
* `import .M` brings in only the name `M` (everything stays qualified).
* `import .M: f` brings in `f` **and** allows adding methods to it.

The last point matters with multiple dispatch: a function belongs to the
module that created it. Adding a method to another module's function needs
either `import .M: f` or, the more common style, a qualified definition
`M.f(x::MyType) = ...` (as with `Base.show` and `Base.iterate` in earlier
units). Defining `f(x::Int) = ...` after `using .M` is an error, because it
would silently create a *different* `f` that hides `M.f`.

examples.caption: `Shapes.area(c::Circle)` adds a method to the module's `area`, so the exported name works for both types.
examples.code:
module Shapes
export Square, area
struct Square
    side::Float64
end
area(s::Square) = s.side^2
end

using .Shapes
struct Circle
    r::Float64
end
Shapes.area(c::Circle) = π * c.r^2
println(area(Square(2.0)), " ", area(Circle(1.0)))
println(length(methods(area)), " methods")

examples.caption: An unqualified definition of a name brought in by `using` is refused.
examples.code:
module Shapes
export area
area(side) = side^2
end

using .Shapes
println(area(3))
area(x::Int) = x
examples.output:
9
ERROR: invalid method definition in Main: function Shapes.area must be explicitly imported to be extended
  @ top-level scope at line 8

examples.caption: `import .M: f` is the other way to say "I am extending M's function".
examples.code:
module Greetings
greet(name::String) = "Hello, $name"
end

import .Greetings: greet
greet(n::Int) = "Hello, visitor number $n"
println(greet("Ada"))
println(Greetings.greet(7))

sections.body:
If two modules you `using` both export the same name, Julia does not pick
one: it prints a warning the first time you use the name, and the
unqualified name is then undefined. Qualify it (`A.greet()`), or bring in
only what you need (`using .A: greet`).

The same happens with packages: `using Statistics` exports `mean`, so a
module of your own that also exports `mean` clashes with it.

examples.code:
module A
export greet
greet() = "hello from A"
end
module B
export greet
greet() = "hello from B"
end

using .A, .B
try
    greet()
catch e
    println(typeof(e))
end
println(A.greet())
println(B.greet())
examples.output:
WARNING: both B and A export "greet"; uses of it in module Main must be qualified
UndefVarError
hello from A
hello from B

sections.body:
A global variable in a module can be rebound to a value of any type at any
time, so the compiler cannot assume its type inside a function: every use
is a dynamic lookup and the result is inferred as `Any`. `const` promises the
binding never changes, so the type is known and functions using it are
fast. Use `const` for module-level tables and parameters; pass changing
values as function arguments.

`Base.return_types` shows what the compiler infers: notice `Any` for the
function that reads the non-constant global.

examples.code:
module Tax
rate = 0.2
const RATE = 0.2
with_global(x) = x * rate
with_const(x) = x * RATE
end

println(Tax.with_global(100.0), " ", Tax.with_const(100.0))
println(Base.return_types(Tax.with_global, (Float64,)))
println(Base.return_types(Tax.with_const, (Float64,)))

sections.title: Constants and globals

sections.body:
Modules nest. Inside a module, `using .Inner` refers to a submodule defined
in the current module and `using ..Sibling` goes one level up first, the same
dots as relative paths.

In a real project each part usually lives in its own file and the top module
stitches them together with `include("util.jl")`. `include` evaluates the
file's code at that point, in the current module, as if pasted there; it
does not create a namespace (that is the `module` keyword's job). A typical
package's `src/MyPkg.jl` is little more than

```julia
module MyPkg
include("util.jl")
include("report.jl")
export summary
end
```

The sandbox runs one file, so the example defines everything inline.

examples.code:
module App
module Util
export clamp01
clamp01(x) = clamp(x, 0, 1)
end

module Report
using ..Util
describe(x) = "value: $(clamp01(x))"
end

using .Util
check(x) = clamp01(x) == x
end

println(App.Report.describe(1.7))
println(App.check(0.5), " ", App.check(-2))
println(parentmodule(App.Util))

sections.title: Submodules and include

sections.body:
A **package** is a module with a `Project.toml` (its name, UUID and
dependencies), distributed so others can `using` it. Three kinds come up:

* **Base**: always loaded (`sum`, `Dict`, `Iterators`).
* **Standard libraries** (stdlib): ship with Julia but must be loaded:
  `using Statistics`, `using Printf`, `using Random`, `using LinearAlgebra`.
  Their version is tied to the Julia version.
* **Registered packages** (DataFrames, CSV, Plots, ...): installed from the
  General registry with the package manager: press `]` in the REPL, then
  `add DataFrames`.

An **environment** is a directory with a `Project.toml` (what you depend on,
optionally with `[compat]` version bounds) and a `Manifest.toml` (the exact
version of every package in the dependency tree, generated by Pkg).
`]activate path` switches environment; `]instantiate` installs exactly what
a Manifest lists. Committing both files is what makes a project
reproducible: anyone gets the same versions.

This course does exactly that. Every unit names an environment in
`course/envs/`: `base` has no packages beyond the standard library, and the
`data` environment's `Project.toml` lists CSV and DataFrames while its
committed `Manifest.toml` pins them (CSV 1.3.0, for example) for Julia
1.10.13.

A package can define a function `__init__()`, which Julia runs each time the
package is loaded (not when it is precompiled): the place for setup that
must happen at runtime, such as reading environment variables or
initializing a C library.

using Statistics

v = [2.0, 4.0, 4.0, 5.0]
@printf("mean %.2f, median %.2f, std %.3f\n", mean(v), median(v), std(v))
println(VERSION)

sections.body:
Julia has two ways to turn a value into text:

* `print` (and `println`, `string`, `"$x"`) writes the value **for humans**:
  a string without its quotes, a character without its single quotes.
* `show` (and `repr`) writes it **as Julia would read it back**: quotes,
  escapes, type information where needed. This is what you see in the REPL
  and in error messages.

The REPL actually calls `show(io, MIME"text/plain"(), x)`, a richer,
possibly multi-line form; `repr(x)` and `show(x)` use the compact one-line
form. Notice the differences in the output below: `print` loses the
information that `"hi"` was a string and `:sym` a symbol, `repr` keeps it.

examples.code:
x = "hi"
print(x); println()
show(x); println()
println(string(x), "  ", repr(x))
println(string('c'), "  ", repr('c'))
println(string(:sym), "  ", repr(:sym))
println("tab\there", "  ", repr("tab\there"))
examples.output:
hi
"hi"
hi  "hi"
c  'c'
sym  :sym
tab	here  "tab\there"

examples.caption: One value, two `show` forms: compact (inside `println` of a vector, and `repr`) and `text/plain` (what the REPL prints).
examples.code:
v = [1.5, 2.0, 3.25]
println(v)
println(repr(v))
show(stdout, MIME"text/plain"(), v)
println()

examples.caption: Defining `Base.show(io, x)` for your type changes how `print`, `repr`, interpolation and containers display it.
examples.code:
struct Point
    x::Int
    y::Int
end
p = Point(1, 2)
println(p)
Base.show(io::IO, p::Point) = print(io, "(", p.x, ", ", p.y, ")")
println(p, "  ", repr(p), "  ", "at $p")
[p, Point(3, 4)]

sections.title: print, show, string and repr

sections.body:
`print` and `write` take an optional first argument: the **stream** to
write to. Besides `stdout` and files, an `IOBuffer` is a stream in memory.
Write pieces into it, then `String(take!(io))` turns the bytes into a
string and empties the buffer.

This is the efficient way to build a long string in a loop. `s *= piece`
copies the whole string every time, so building `n` pieces that way costs
time proportional to `n²` (the `format-number-column` problem measures it).

`sprint(f, args...)` is the shortcut: it creates the buffer, calls
`f(io, args...)` and returns the string.

examples.code:
io = IOBuffer()
write(io, "abc")
print(io, 42, ' ', 3.5)
println(io, "!")
s = String(take!(io))
println(repr(s))
println(isempty(take!(io)))
println(sprint(show, "quoted"))
println(sprint(io -> join(io, 1:5, " + ")))

sections.title: Building text in an IOBuffer

sections.body:
The `Printf` standard library gives C-style formatting: `@printf` prints and
`@sprintf` returns a string. A format spec is `%[flags][width][.precision]type`:

* types: `d` integer, `f` fixed-point, `e` scientific, `g` shortest, `s`
  anything printed with `print`, `x` hexadecimal;
* width pads to at least that many characters, right-aligned; the flag `-`
  aligns left and `0` pads with zeros; `+` always shows the sign;
* `.2f` means two digits after the decimal point (rounded, not truncated).

`@printf(io, ...)` writes to any stream, an `IOBuffer` included. The format
must be a literal string: it is compiled by the macro.

examples.caption: Fixed widths line up columns.
examples.code:
using Printf
for (name, qty, price) in [("apple", 3, 0.5), ("watermelon", 1, 4.25), ("fig", 12, 0.333)]
    @printf("%-10s %4d %8.2f\n", name, qty, price)
end

sections.body:
`open(path, "w") do io ... end` opens a file for writing, runs the block
with the stream `io`, and closes the file afterwards, even if the block
throws (the `do` + `finally` pattern from the errors unit). The modes:
`"r"` read (the default), `"w"` write (creates the file or **truncates** it),
`"a"` append to the end.

To read: `read(path, String)` returns the whole file, `readlines(path)` a
vector of lines without their newlines, and `eachline(path)` iterates over
the lines lazily, which is what you want for large files. `write(path, s)`
writes a whole string in one call.

`mktempdir()` creates a fresh temporary directory (removed when Julia exits),
which keeps examples from touching your own files. Its path differs on every
run and every system, so the examples print file *contents*, never paths.

examples.code:
dir = mktempdir()
path = joinpath(dir, "notes.txt")
open(path, "w") do io
    println(io, "first line")
    println(io, "second line")
end
open(path, "a") do io
    println(io, "appended")
end
print(read(path, String))
println(readlines(path))
for (i, line) in enumerate(eachline(path))
    println(i, ": ", line)
end
println(countlines(path), " lines, ", filesize(path), " bytes")
examples.output:
first line
second line
appended
["first line", "second line", "appended"]
1: first line
2: second line
3: appended
3 lines, 32 bytes

examples.caption: Mode `"w"` replaces what was there; `write(path, s)` returns the number of bytes written.
examples.code:
path = joinpath(mktempdir(), "data.txt")
println(write(path, "old content\n"))
open(path, "w") do io
    print(io, "new")
end
read(path, String)

sections.body:
`print(x)` is `print(stdout, x)`. A program has a second output stream,
`stderr`, for diagnostics: `println(stderr, "warning: ...")`. Keeping
messages on `stderr` means the real output on `stdout` can be piped into a
file or another program without them. `@warn` and `@info` log to `stderr`.

`write(io, x)` writes raw bytes (for a string, its UTF-8 encoding) and
returns how many it wrote; `print` writes the text form. For strings the
result looks the same, but the count shows that `é` takes two bytes.
`redirect_stdout(f, io)` runs `f` with `stdout` pointed elsewhere (here
`devnull`, which discards everything), which is useful in tests.

examples.code:
n = write(stdout, "héllo\n")
println(n, " bytes for ", length("héllo\n"), " characters")
redirect_stdout(devnull) do
    println("this line goes nowhere")
end
println("back on stdout")
examples.output:
héllo
7 bytes for 6 characters
back on stdout

sections.body:
For small, regular formats `split` and `parse` go a long way. `split(s, ',')`
returns `SubString`s (views into `s`, no copying); `strip` removes surrounding
whitespace; `parse(Int, s)` and `parse(Float64, s)` convert, throwing on bad
input (or use `tryparse`). `eachline(IOBuffer(text))` iterates over the lines
of a string just as `eachline(path)` does for a file.

Hand parsing is fine for configuration files and quick scripts; for real CSV
(quoted fields, embedded commas, missing values) use the CSV.jl package
(the data unit).

examples.code:
text = """
name,qty,price
apple,3,0.5
pear,10,0.25
fig,2,1.75
"""
lines = readlines(IOBuffer(text))
header = split(lines[1], ',')
total = 0.0
for line in lines[2:end]
    name, qty, price = split(line, ',')
    total += parse(Int, qty) * parse(Float64, price)
end
println(header, "  ", typeof(header))
println("total = ", total)

sections.body:
Julia compiles a function the first time you call it with a given combination
of argument types. So the **first** call of anything measures the compiler as
much as your code: `@time` reports that share as "compilation time". Always
call once to warm up, then measure, and repeat the measurement a few times and
keep the minimum (the least disturbed run). The package
[BenchmarkTools.jl](https://juliaci.github.io/BenchmarkTools.jl/stable/)
automates this with `@btime` and `@benchmark`; here we stay with Base.

Timings change from run to run and machine to machine, so the timing examples
on this page are recorded but not checked (the numbers you see are from one
run). Allocations are different: `@allocated` counts the bytes a call
allocates, and once the function is compiled that number is deterministic.
Measure it **inside a function**, after a warm-up call: at global scope the
measurement also counts the work of handling untyped global variables.

Later sections use a one-line helper for this:

```julia
measure(f::F, args...) where {F} = (f(args...); @allocated f(args...))
```

The `f::F ... where {F}` matters. Julia's heuristics sometimes decline to
specialise a method on a `Function` argument (here: one called with splatted
arguments), and the unspecialised call boxes its result. The type parameter
forces a specialised version, so the helper adds nothing to the count; written
as `measure(f, args...)` it reports 16 extra bytes for every call. The
[performance tips](https://docs.julialang.org/en/v1/manual/performance-tips/#Be-aware-of-when-Julia-avoids-specializing)
explain when this happens.

examples.caption: The first `@time` includes compiling `f`; the second is the work alone. Recorded, not checked: timings vary.
examples.output:
0.058258 seconds (28.08 k allocations: 1.935 MiB, 98.80% compilation time)
  0.000623 seconds (1 allocation: 16 bytes)
best of 20 runs: 196.1 μs

examples.caption: `@allocated` inside a function, after warming up: deterministic, so this output is checked.

sections.title: Measuring without fooling yourself

sections.body:
A function is **type-stable** when the type of its result follows from the
types of its arguments alone, never from their values. Then the compiler knows
the type of every intermediate value and emits specialised machine code. When
it cannot know, it has to box values and look methods up at run time.

`Base.return_types(f, (ArgTypes...,))` asks the compiler what `f` returns. In
the REPL, `@code_warntype f(args...)` shows the inferred type of every local
variable and highlights the abstract ones (its output is long, so it is not
shown here; try it on your own functions).

The classic mistake is a literal of the wrong type: `0` is an `Int`, so a
function that returns `0` on one branch and a `Float64` on another returns a
`Union`. The fix is to build the constant from the argument: `zero(x)`,
`one(x)`, `zero(eltype(v))`. The same mistake hides in accumulators: `s = 0`
followed by `s += x` for floats makes `s` an `Int` before the loop and a
`Float64` after it, and an empty input returns the `Int`.

examples.caption: The return type depends on the *value* of `x`; `zero(x)` fixes it.
examples.code:
clamp_negative(x) = x < 0 ? 0 : x
clamp_negative_stable(x) = x < 0 ? zero(x) : x
println(Base.return_types(clamp_negative, (Float64,)))
println(Base.return_types(clamp_negative_stable, (Float64,)))
println(typeof(clamp_negative(-1.5)), " ", typeof(clamp_negative(1.5)))

examples.caption: An accumulator that starts as `0` and becomes a `Float64`; notice what the empty vector returns.
examples.code:
function total(v)
    s = 0                  # an Int ...
    for x in v
        s += x             # ... that becomes a Float64
    end
    return s
end
function total_stable(v)
    s = zero(eltype(v))    # 0.0 for a Vector{Float64}
    for x in v
        s += x
    end
    return s
end
println(Base.return_types(total, (Vector{Float64},)))
println(Base.return_types(total_stable, (Vector{Float64},)))
println(repr(total(Float64[])), "  ", repr(total_stable(Float64[])))

sections.title: Type stability

sections.body:
A non-`const` global variable can be rebound to a value of any type at any
moment, so a function that reads it cannot assume anything about its type:
the result is inferred as `Any`, and every operation on it is a dynamic
lookup. This is why "put your code in functions" is the first performance tip
in the [manual](https://docs.julialang.org/en/v1/manual/performance-tips/).
Three fixes, from most to least common:

* pass the value as an **argument** (the function is then compiled for its type);
* declare it `const` if it really never changes;
* give the global a **type** (Julia 1.8 and later): `rate::Float64 = 1.5`. Its
  value can still change, but only to another `Float64`.

Python and MATLAB users write scripts full of top-level loops over globals;
in Julia the same loop inside a function is often tens of times faster.

examples.caption: Reading an untyped global makes the result `Any`; `const` or an argument makes it concrete.

sections.body:
A `Vector{Float64}` stores the numbers themselves, side by side in memory. A
`Vector{Any}` or a `Vector{Real}` stores *pointers* to boxed values, because
its elements may have different types and sizes; every access then follows a
pointer and dispatches at run time. `isconcretetype` tells you whether a type
can be the type of an actual value: `Float64` can, `Real` cannot.

The same applies to struct fields. A field declared `x::Real` can hold any
real number, so code that reads it cannot be specialised. Make the struct
**parametric** instead: `struct Point{T<:Real}; x::T; end` creates a separate
concrete type `Point{Float64}`, `Point{Int64}`, … for each field type, with
the same flexibility and none of the cost.

println("Vector{Float64}: ", measure(sum, a), " bytes")
println("Vector{Any} allocates:  ", measure(sum, b) > 0)
println("Vector{Real} allocates: ", measure(sum, c) > 0)

sections.body:
Allocating memory is not free, and the garbage collector must later reclaim
it. Three sources dominate in numerical code.

**Slices copy.** Unlike NumPy, `x[2:end-1]` creates a new array (MATLAB and R
copy too). `@view x[2:end-1]` creates a lightweight window into `x` instead,
and `@views` in front of a function or block turns every slice in it into a
view. Mutating a view mutates the parent.

**Every vectorised operation makes an array**, unless you fuse it. `2x + x.^2`
makes three arrays (one per operation); the dotted `2 .* x .+ x .^ 2` fuses
into a single loop with a single result array; and `out .= 2 .* x .+ x .^ 2`
(or `@. out = 2x + x^2`) writes into an existing array and allocates nothing.

**Preallocate and update in place.** Functions whose names end in `!` modify
an argument instead of returning a new value: `mul!(C, A, B)` from
`LinearAlgebra` writes `A * B` into `C`, `sort!`, `push!`, `copyto!`, `fill!`.
In a loop that runs many times, allocate the output once outside it.

In the last example a 1000-element `Vector{Float64}` costs 8128 bytes (8000
for the data plus the array header): the unfused version allocates three of
them, the fused one a single array (plus 16 bytes of bookkeeping), the
in-place one nothing; `A * B` allocates the 50×50 result, `mul!` nothing.

examples.caption: A slice is a copy; a view is a window into the original array.
examples.code:

s = x[2:4]          # a new array
v = @view x[2:4]    # a view of x
s[1] = 100          # changes only the copy
v[2] = 300          # changes x[3]
x

println(measure(inner_sum_copy, x), " ", measure(inner_sum_view, x), " ", measure(inner_sum_views, x))

sections.body:
Loops are fast in Julia (unlike in Python or R there is no need to vectorise
for speed), but the processor still rewards some habits.

**Arrays are column-major**, like Fortran and MATLAB and unlike C and NumPy's
default: `A[1,1]`, `A[2,1]`, `A[3,1]`, … are adjacent in memory. Make the
*first* index vary fastest, i.e. put the row loop inside the column loop.
Walking along rows jumps through memory and wastes most of every cache line
fetched; the gap grows with the matrix.

**Do not repeat work in the inner loop.** A value that does not change inside
the loop (a norm, a length, a lookup) belongs before it. Recomputing an O(n)
quantity n times turns an O(n) function into an O(n²) one.

**`@inbounds` and `@simd`.** Every `x[i]` checks that `i` is a valid index.
`@inbounds` removes the check, and `@simd` lets the compiler reorder a
reduction so it can use vector instructions (so a floating-point sum may
differ in the last bits). Write and test the bounds-checked version first:
with checks on, a wrong index is a `BoundsError`; under `@inbounds` it is
**undefined behaviour**, i.e. garbage results or a crash, not an error. Prefer
`eachindex(x)` over `1:length(x)`: it is always valid, so the compiler can
often drop the checks by itself.

examples.caption: `vec` shows the memory order: down the first column, then the second.
The same sum, two loop orders, on a 2000×2000 matrix. Recorded, not checked: timings vary.
examples.code:
function sum_by_columns(A)
    s = zero(eltype(A))
    for j in axes(A, 2), i in axes(A, 1)    # i (rows) varies fastest
        s += A[i, j]
    end
    return s
end
function sum_by_rows(A)
    s = zero(eltype(A))
    for i in axes(A, 1), j in axes(A, 2)    # j varies fastest: strided access
        s += A[i, j]
    end
    return s
end
A = rand(2000, 2000)
sum_by_columns(A); sum_by_rows(A)
t_col = minimum(@elapsed(sum_by_columns(A)) for _ in 1:5)
t_row = minimum(@elapsed(sum_by_rows(A)) for _ in 1:5)
println("columns: ", round(t_col * 1e3; digits = 1), " ms, rows: ", round(t_row * 1e3; digits = 1), " ms")

examples.caption: A norm recomputed inside the loop makes the function quadratic. Same result, very different time (not checked).
examples.code:
function normalize_slow(v)
    out = similar(v)
    for i in eachindex(v)
        out[i] = v[i] / sqrt(sum(abs2, v))   # O(n) work, n times
    end
    return out
end
function normalize_fast(v)
    nrm = sqrt(sum(abs2, v))                # once, before the loop
    out = similar(v)
    for i in eachindex(v)
        out[i] = v[i] / nrm
    end
    return out
end
v = rand(20_000)
println(normalize_slow(v) == normalize_fast(v))
t_slow = @elapsed normalize_slow(v)
t_fast = @elapsed normalize_fast(v)
println("slow: ", round(t_slow * 1e3; digits = 2), " ms, fast: ", round(t_fast * 1e3; digits = 3), " ms")
