sections.body:
Sometimes a type really is unknown until run time: a value read from a file,
a `Dict{String,Any}` of columns, a user's choice. You cannot make that one
lookup type-stable, but you can stop the uncertainty from spreading. Do the
lookup in a small outer function and hand the value to a **kernel function**
that does the real work. Calling the kernel costs one dynamic dispatch; inside
it, Julia compiles a specialised version for the actual type, so the loop is
fast. This pattern is called a *function barrier*.

In the example, `sum_of_column` loops over a value of type `Any`; `kernel` is
inferred concretely for a `Vector{Float64}`, and `sum_with_barrier` only adds
one dispatch in front of it. (Timings recorded, not checked.)

examples.code:
function sum_of_column(table::Dict{String,Any}, name)
    col = table[name]                 # type known only at run time
    s = zero(eltype(col))
    for x in col                      # every step is a dynamic call
        s += x
    end
    return s
end
function kernel(col)
    s = zero(eltype(col))
    for x in col
        s += x
    end
    return s
end
sum_with_barrier(table, name) = kernel(table[name])

table = Dict{String,Any}("price" => rand(10^6), "count" => rand(1:9, 10^6))
println(Base.return_types(sum_of_column, (Dict{String,Any}, String)))
println(Base.return_types(kernel, (Vector{Float64},)))
println(sum_of_column(table, "price") == sum_with_barrier(table, "price"))
sum_of_column(table, "price"); sum_with_barrier(table, "price")
t1 = minimum(@elapsed(sum_of_column(table, "price")) for _ in 1:5)
t2 = minimum(@elapsed(sum_with_barrier(table, "price")) for _ in 1:5)
println("no barrier: ", round(t1 * 1e3; digits = 2), " ms, barrier: ", round(t2 * 1e3; digits = 2), " ms")

true

sections.body:
A method signature can name the types it receives: in
`f(v::AbstractVector{T}) where {T}` the *type parameter* `T` is bound to the
element type of the argument, and you can use it in the body like any value.
`where {T<:Real}` restricts it. Writing the same parameter twice,
`f(x::T, y::T) where {T}`, means "both arguments have the same type".

One rule surprises everyone: parametric types are **invariant**. A
`Vector{Int}` is *not* a `Vector{Real}`, even though `Int <: Real`, because a
`Vector{Real}` is a specific container that can hold any mix of reals (see the
performance unit for why it is slow). To accept "a vector of any real type",
write `AbstractVector{<:Real}`, short for `AbstractVector{T} where {T<:Real}`.

sections.body:
Coming from C or Java, it is tempting to annotate every argument. In Julia it
does not make the code faster: the compiler specialises a method for the
concrete types it is *called* with, annotated or not. `double(x) = 2x`
called with a `Float64` compiles to the same single multiplication as
`double(x::Float64) = 2x`, and it keeps working for integers, rationals,
`BigFloat`s and types that do not exist yet.

Annotate to **choose between methods** (dispatch), or to document and
reject what makes no sense. Over-narrow annotations such as `::Float64` or
`::Vector{Float64}` are a common reason a package refuses an `Int`, a range,
a view or a `Float32` that would have worked.

sections.body:
`struct Interval{T<:Real}` defines a family of concrete types,
`Interval{Int64}`, `Interval{Float64}`, …, with concretely typed fields.
Constructors come in two kinds:

* an **inner constructor** (inside the `struct`, calling `new`) is the only
  way to create the object, so it is the place to enforce an invariant such as
  `lo ≤ hi`;
* **outer constructors** are ordinary methods that add conveniences: here
  `Interval(1, 3)` infers `T` from the arguments, and `Interval(1, 2.5)`
  promotes mixed arguments to a common type first.

Once you write an inner constructor, Julia no longer defines the default
ones, which is why the outer `Interval(lo::T, hi::T)` is needed.

examples.code:
struct Interval{T<:Real}
    lo::T
    hi::T
    function Interval{T}(lo, hi) where {T<:Real}
        lo <= hi || throw(ArgumentError("need lo ≤ hi, got $lo > $hi"))
        return new{T}(lo, hi)
    end
end
Interval(lo::T, hi::T) where {T<:Real} = Interval{T}(lo, hi)
Interval(lo::Real, hi::Real) = Interval(promote(lo, hi)...)
width(i::Interval) = i.hi - i.lo

println(width(Interval(1//2, 3//4)))

sections.body:
Arithmetic between different types in Julia goes through **promotion**:
`1 + 2.5` has no special method; the fallback `+(x::Number, y::Number)` calls
`promote(x, y)` to convert both to a common type, then adds those. To make
your own type join in, write

* the operations between two values of your type (`Base.:+`, `Base.:*`, …);
* `Base.promote_rule(::Type{Mine}, ::Type{Other})`: the common type;
* `Base.convert(::Type{Mine}, x::Other)`: how to convert.

You extend Base's functions (`Base.:+`), you do not shadow them; that is how
`sum`, `prod`, `^` and every generic algorithm start working on the new type.
Below, integers modulo `N` with `N` a type parameter: `Mod{7}` and `Mod{5}`
are different types, and mixing them is an error (no promotion rule
between them) rather than a silent bug.

examples.caption: Operations between two `Mod{N}` values work; `a + 1` fails because there is no promotion rule yet: `promote` cannot find a common type.
examples.code:
struct Mod{N} <: Number
    val::Int
    Mod{N}(x::Integer) where {N} = new(mod(x, N))
end
Base.:+(a::Mod{N}, b::Mod{N}) where {N} = Mod{N}(a.val + b.val)
Base.:*(a::Mod{N}, b::Mod{N}) where {N} = Mod{N}(a.val * b.val)
Base.show(io::IO, a::Mod{N}) where {N} = print(io, a.val, " (mod ", N, ")")

a = Mod{7}(5)
println(a + Mod{7}(4), ", ", a * a)
a + 1

ERROR: promotion of types Mod{7} and Int64 failed to change any arguments

examples.code:

    val::Int
    Mod{N}(x::Integer) where {N} = new(mod(x, N))
end
Base.:+(a::Mod{N}, b::Mod{N}) where {N} = Mod{N}(a.val + b.val)
Base.:*(a::Mod{N}, b::Mod{N}) where {N} = Mod{N}(a.val * b.val)

sections.body:
Julia supports two styles of generic code, and good code uses both.

**Duck typing**: leave arguments unannotated and use only the operations you
need. `describe(x)` below calls `length` and `first`, so it works for arrays,
strings, tuples, dicts, even a number (numbers are iterable collections of one
element), with no declaration anywhere.

**Dispatch on abstract types** picks a method by what a type *is*:
`AbstractVector`, `AbstractString`, `Number`. But a type has only one
supertype, and many properties cut across the hierarchy ("is it sorted?",
"is its length known?"). For those Julia uses **Holy traits** (after Tim
Holy): a function from a *type* to a small singleton object, and methods that
dispatch on that object. Base does this with `Base.IteratorSize`, which
`collect` uses to decide whether it can preallocate. The trait is computed from
the type, so the compiler resolves the choice at compile time: there is no
run-time check left.

examples.code:
describe(x) = "$(length(x)) item(s), first: $(repr(first(x)))"
println(describe([3, 1, 2]))
println(describe("hello"))
println(describe((a = 1, b = 2)))
println(describe(42))
examples.output:
3 item(s), first: 3
5 item(s), first: 'h'
2 item(s), first: 1
1 item(s), first: 42

examples.caption: Base's trait: what `collect` knows about an iterator's length.
examples.code:
println(Base.IteratorSize([1, 2, 3]))
println(Base.IteratorSize(x^2 for x in 1:3))
println(Base.IteratorSize(Iterators.filter(iseven, 1:10)))
println(Base.IteratorSize(Iterators.countfrom(1)))

examples.caption: A custom trait: ranges declare themselves sorted, so `mymedian` skips the sort for them.
examples.code:
abstract type Sortedness end
struct KnownSorted <: Sortedness end
struct MaybeUnsorted <: Sortedness end
sortedness(::Type) = MaybeUnsorted()
sortedness(::Type{<:AbstractRange}) = KnownSorted()

mymedian(x) = mymedian(sortedness(typeof(x)), x)
function mymedian(::KnownSorted, x)
    n = length(x)
    return (x[(n + 1) ÷ 2] + x[n ÷ 2 + 1]) / 2
end
mymedian(::MaybeUnsorted, x) = mymedian(KnownSorted(), sort(x))

println(sortedness(typeof(1:10)), " ", sortedness(typeof([3, 1, 2])))
println(mymedian(1:10), " ", mymedian([5, 1, 4]), " ", mymedian([7, 1, 3, 2]))

sections.body:
`Val(3)` is an instance of the type `Val{3}`: it moves a value into the type
domain, so methods can dispatch on it and the compiler can treat it as a
constant. `ntuple(f, Val(4))` builds a tuple whose length is known at compile
time; `Val(:fast)` can select an algorithm by name.

Use it only when the value is a **literal at the call site**. `Val(n)` with an
`n` computed at run time creates a type the compiler could not predict, so the
call becomes a dynamic dispatch and is slower than an ordinary argument. For
most choices a plain argument or a keyword is the right tool.

examples.code:

power(x, ::Val{N}) where {N} = x^N
println(power(2.0, Val(3)))
algorithm(::Val{:fast}, x) = "fast path for $x"
algorithm(::Val{:safe}, x) = "safe path for $x"
println(algorithm(Val(:fast), 1))
algorithm(Val(:other), 1)

sections.body:
Before Julia runs your code it parses it into a data structure you can
inspect and build yourself. A **`Symbol`** is an interned name: `:x` is the
symbol `x` (and `Symbol("x")` makes the same one). An **`Expr`** has a
`head` saying what kind of expression it is (`:call`, `:(=)`, `:block`,
`:if`, …) and a vector `args` of sub-expressions, which can be symbols,
literals or further `Expr`s.

`Meta.parse` turns a string into an expression, and `dump` prints the tree.
Notice that an operator call `a + 1` is just a `:call` whose first argument is
the function's name `:+`.

examples.code:
ex = Meta.parse("a + b * 2")
println(typeof(ex), " ", ex.head, " ", ex.args)
println(typeof(:a), " ", :a === Symbol("a"))
dump(:(a + 1))
examples.output:
Expr call Any[:+, :a, :(b * 2)]
Symbol true
Expr
  head: Symbol call
  args: Array{Any}((3,))
    1: Symbol +
    2: Symbol a
    3: Int64 1

sections.title: Symbols and expressions

sections.body:
`:( ... )` *quotes* code: it returns the expression instead of evaluating it.
For several lines, `quote ... end` does the same and produces a `:block`
expression; it also records source positions as `LineNumberNode`s (the
`#= main.jl:3 =#` comments in the display), which
`Base.remove_linenums!` strips.

Inside a quote, `$` **interpolates**: `:($x + 1)` puts the *value* of `x`
into the expression, while `:(x + 1)` keeps the symbol. `$(args...)` splices
a list of arguments. You can also build expressions directly with
`Expr(head, args...)`, which is what quoting does for you.

examples.code:
ex1 = :(x + 1)
ex2 = quote
    y = x + 1
    y * 2
end
println(typeof(ex1), " ", ex1.head, " ", ex2.head)
ex2
examples.output:
Expr call block
quote
    #= main.jl:3 =#
    y = x + 1
    #= main.jl:4 =#
    y * 2
end

examples.code:
x = 10
println(:(x + 1), "   ", :($x + 1))
args = [:a, :b, :c]
println(:(f($(args...))))
println(Expr(:call, :+, 1, 2) == :(1 + 2))

sections.title: Quoting and interpolation

sections.body:
`eval(ex)` evaluates an expression **in the global scope of the current
module**. At the top level that is useful: it can define variables or
functions whose names are computed (`eval(:($name = 42)))`).

Inside a function `eval` is almost always a mistake. It cannot see the
function's local variables (they do not exist in global scope), it compiles
the expression anew on every call, and its result has a type the compiler
cannot know. If you find yourself writing `eval` inside a function, you
usually want a closure, a `Dict` from names to functions, or dispatch.

examples.code:
ex = :(2 + 3 * 4)
println(eval(ex))
name = :answer
eval(:($name = 42))
answer

sections.body:
A **macro** is a function that runs when the code is *parsed*: it receives
its arguments as expressions (unevaluated) and returns a new expression that
replaces the macro call. `@macroexpand` shows that replacement, which is the
first thing to look at when a macro misbehaves.

Macros are **hygienic**: variables that the macro's own code assigns are
renamed (to fresh names from `gensym`) so they cannot clash with the
caller's, and other names are looked up in the module where the macro was
defined. Code that comes from the *caller* must be wrapped in `esc(...)` so
that it keeps its meaning in the caller's scope. Forgetting `esc` is the
classic macro bug. In the second example the unescaped `x` in `x *= 3` is
resolved in the macro's module, as the global `Main.x`, and an expansion may
not assign to a module-qualified name: the error points at the macro call.

examples.code:
macro twice(ex)
    return quote
        $(esc(ex))
        $(esc(ex))
    end
end
x = 1
@twice x *= 3
println(x)
Base.remove_linenums!(@macroexpand @twice x *= 3)

examples.caption: Without `esc`, the caller's `x` is read as a name in the macro's module.
examples.code:
macro twice_unescaped(ex)
    return quote
        $ex
        $ex
    end
end
x = 1
@twice_unescaped x *= 3
examples.output:
ERROR: syntax: invalid assignment location "Main.x" around main.jl:3
  @ top-level scope at line 8

examples.caption: Hygiene protects the caller: the macro's own `n` is a different variable.
examples.code:
macro repeat3(ex)
    return quote
        n = 0
        for _ in 1:3
            $(esc(ex))
            n += 1
        end
        n
    end
end
n = 100
r = @repeat3 print("hi ")
println()
println(r, " ", n)

sections.title: Macros, esc and hygiene

sections.body:
Macros earn their place when they need the *code itself*, not only its
value: to skip evaluating it, to evaluate it differently, or to print it.
`@unless cond body` evaluates `body` only when `cond` is false, which no
function can do (a function's arguments are evaluated before it is called).
`@logcall f(args...)` prints the call as written in the source together with
the argument values, then makes the call. Note how it checks its input and
raises a clear error at expansion time for anything that is not a call.

examples.code:
macro logcall(ex)
    (ex isa Expr && ex.head == :call) || error("@logcall expects a function call, got $(repr(ex))")
    f = ex.args[1]
    args = ex.args[2:end]
    return quote
        local vals = ($(map(esc, args)...),)
        println("call ", $(string(ex)), " with ", vals)
        $(esc(f))(vals...)
    end
end
a = 3
r = @logcall max(a, 2a + 1)
println("result ", r)
@logcall a + 1
@logcall 42
examples.output:
call max(a, 2a + 1) with (3, 7)
result 7
call a + 1 with (3, 1)
ERROR: @logcall expects a function call, got 42
  @ @logcall at line 2

sections.title: Small useful macros

sections.body:
A macro is harder to read, to debug and to compose than a function, so use a
function whenever the *values* are all you need. A macro that pastes its
argument twice also **evaluates it twice**, with every side effect: below,
`@square(next!())` calls `next!` twice and multiplies two different numbers,
while the function `square` evaluates its argument once. Julia's compiler
already inlines small functions, so a macro is never needed "for speed".

examples.code:
macro square(ex)
    return :($(esc(ex)) * $(esc(ex)))
end
square(x) = x * x
counter = 0
next!() = (global counter += 1; counter)
println(@square(next!()), " after ", counter, " calls")
counter = 0
println(square(next!()), " after ", counter, " call")

sections.body:
`@eval expr` is `eval(:(expr))` with interpolation: a loop over symbols can
define many similar methods at once. This is how Base defines arithmetic for
its many number types, and it is the right tool when the methods differ only
in a name or an operator. The loop runs once, at load time; the generated
methods are ordinary compiled methods, with no run-time cost.

sections.body:
Julia has no `interface` keyword. An interface is a documented list of methods
(see [Interfaces](https://docs.julialang.org/en/v1/manual/interfaces/) in the
manual): implement them for your type and every generic function written
against the interface works with it.

The **iteration** interface is the smallest. `for x in itr` is rewritten to

```julia
next = iterate(itr)
while next !== nothing
    (x, state) = next
    # loop body
    next = iterate(itr, state)
end
```

so you define `Base.iterate(itr)` and `Base.iterate(itr, state)`, each
returning `(item, next_state)` or `nothing` at the end. Optional methods tell
generic code more: `Base.length` (and `Base.IteratorSize` when the length is
unknown), and `Base.eltype` so that `collect` can allocate the right array.
Then `collect`, `sum`, `maximum`, comprehensions, `first(itr, n)`, `zip`, …
all work.

examples.code:
struct Countdown
    from::Int
end
Base.iterate(c::Countdown, n = c.from) = n < 1 ? nothing : (n, n - 1)
Base.length(c::Countdown) = max(c.from, 0)
Base.eltype(::Type{Countdown}) = Int

for k in Countdown(3)
    print(k, " ")
end
println()
println(collect(Countdown(4)), " ", sum(Countdown(10)), " ", maximum(Countdown(5)))
println([2k for k in Countdown(3)], " ", first(Countdown(9), 2), " ", collect(zip(Countdown(2), "ab")))

sections.title: Informal interfaces: iteration

sections.body:
Subtype `AbstractArray{T,N}` (or `AbstractVector{T}`, `AbstractMatrix{T}`)
and define two methods:

* `Base.size(A)`: a tuple of dimensions;
* `Base.getindex(A, i::Int)` for a vector, or `getindex(A, i::Int, j::Int, …)`
  with one index per dimension.

That is enough for display, iteration, `sum`, broadcasting, `findfirst`,
slicing, comparisons with `==`, and most of LinearAlgebra. Optional extras:
`Base.setindex!` for a mutable array, and `Base.IndexStyle(::Type{<:MyArray})
= IndexLinear()` when one linear index is the natural way to address the
elements (then you define `getindex(A, i::Int)` even for a matrix). Lazy arrays
compute elements on demand: below, a one-hot vector stores two integers
instead of `n` values, and a multiplication table stores one.

Check the index yourself in `getindex`: `@boundscheck checkbounds(A, i)` raises
a `BoundsError` and lets a caller's `@inbounds` remove the check.

examples.code:
struct OneHot <: AbstractVector{Bool}
    n::Int
    k::Int
end
Base.size(v::OneHot) = (v.n,)
function Base.getindex(v::OneHot, i::Int)
    @boundscheck checkbounds(v, i)
    return i == v.k
end

v = OneHot(5, 2)
println(sum(v), " ", findfirst(v), " ", v == [false, true, false, false, false])
println(v .* 10, " ", [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]' * v)
v

struct Times <: AbstractMatrix{Int}
    n::Int
end
Base.size(t::Times) = (t.n, t.n)
Base.IndexStyle(::Type{Times}) = IndexLinear()
function Base.getindex(t::Times, i::Int)
    @boundscheck checkbounds(t, i)
    col, row = fldmod1(i, t.n)    # column-major: column = fld1(i, n), row = mod1(i, n)
    return row * col
end

sections.body:
Two methods control how a value is printed:

* `Base.show(io::IO, x::T)`: the **compact**, one-line form used by `print`,
  `string`, `repr`, string interpolation and inside containers. Ideally it
  looks like code that would recreate the value.
* `Base.show(io::IO, ::MIME"text/plain", x::T)`: the **rich** form the REPL
  (and this site) uses to display a value on its own. It may span several
  lines. If you define only the first, it is used for both.

Do not overload `print` or `display` for this; `show` is the interface they
both call. `get(io, :compact, false)` tells you when the caller asked for an
especially short form (e.g. inside a matrix).

examples.code:
struct Money
    cents::Int
    currency::String
end
amount(m::Money) = string(m.cents ÷ 100, ".", lpad(m.cents % 100, 2, '0'))
Base.show(io::IO, m::Money) = print(io, m.currency, " ", amount(m))
Base.show(io::IO, ::MIME"text/plain", m::Money) =
    print(io, "Money: ", amount(m), " ", m.currency, " (", m.cents, " cents)")

m = Money(1999, "EUR")
println(m)
println([m, Money(5, "EUR")])
println(repr(m), " | ", "price: $m")
m

Money[EUR 19.99, EUR 0.05]

sections.body:
**Ordering**: define `Base.isless(a::T, b::T)` and `sort`, `sort!`,
`maximum`, `minimum`, `extrema`, `searchsorted` and `<` all work, because
they are written in terms of `isless`. Comparing tuples lexicographically is
a short way to get it right for several fields.

**AbstractDict**: subtype `AbstractDict{K,V}` and define `Base.get(d, k,
default)`, `Base.iterate` and `Base.length`; then `d[k]`, `haskey`, `keys`,
`values`, `pairs` and display work. Below, a read-only dictionary of HTTP
headers that ignores the case of its keys.

examples.code:
struct Version
    major::Int
    minor::Int
    patch::Int
end
Base.isless(a::Version, b::Version) = isless((a.major, a.minor, a.patch), (b.major, b.minor, b.patch))
Base.show(io::IO, v::Version) = print(io, "v", v.major, ".", v.minor, ".", v.patch)

vs = [Version(1, 2, 0), Version(1, 10, 1), Version(0, 9, 9)]
println(sort(vs), " ", maximum(vs), " ", Version(1, 2, 0) < Version(1, 10, 0))

struct Headers <: AbstractDict{String,String}
    data::Dict{String,String}
end
Headers(ps::Pair{String,String}...) = Headers(Dict(lowercase(k) => v for (k, v) in ps))
Base.get(h::Headers, k::AbstractString, default) = get(h.data, lowercase(k), default)
Base.iterate(h::Headers, state...) = iterate(h.data, state...)
Base.length(h::Headers) = length(h.data)

h = Headers("Content-Type" => "text/html", "Accept" => "*/*")
println(h["ACCEPT"], " ", haskey(h, "content-type"), " ", get(h, "X-Missing", "none"), " ", length(h))
h["Cookie"]

sections.body:
An informal interface is often implemented half-way, so test it. The `Test`
standard library provides `@test expr` (passes when `expr` is `true`) and
`@test_throws ExceptionType expr`; `@testset "name" begin ... end` groups
tests and prints a summary. Test the *generic* functions that your methods are
supposed to enable, not only the methods themselves: that is what the
interface promises.

A `@test` outside a test set prints `Test Passed`, or the failing expression
with its evaluated values and then throws an error (inside a test set,
failures are counted instead and reported in the summary). A test set prints one summary line with the counts
and the time taken (so that example's output is recorded, not checked).

examples.code:
using Test
@test sum(1:4) == 10

sections.body:
A **task** (also called a coroutine or green thread) is a piece of work that
can be paused and resumed. `@async expr` wraps `expr` in a `Task`, schedules
it, and returns the task immediately, without waiting. `fetch(t)` waits for
the task to finish and returns its value; `wait(t)` waits without returning the
value; `istaskdone(t)` asks whether it has finished.

A task only runs when the current one *yields*: when it waits (`fetch`,
`wait`, `sleep`, I/O, `take!` on an empty channel) or calls `yield()`. Notice
in the first example that the task is not done when we first ask: it has not
even had a chance to start yet.

examples.code:
t = @async begin
    sleep(0.01)
    21 * 2
end
println(istaskdone(t))
println(fetch(t))
println(istaskdone(t))

examples.caption: `@async` is shorthand for creating a `Task` and calling `schedule` on it.
examples.code:
t = Task(() -> println("hello from inside the task"))
println(istaskstarted(t))   # created, but not scheduled yet
schedule(t)
wait(t)
println(istaskdone(t))
examples.output:
false
hello from inside the task
true

examples.caption: Tasks finish in any order, but `fetch` in a fixed order gives a deterministic result. Here the last task finishes first.
examples.code:
tasks = [@async (sleep(0.01 * (4 - i)); i^2) for i in 1:3]
fetch.(tasks)

examples.caption: An error inside a task surfaces when you `fetch` it, wrapped in a `TaskFailedException`.
examples.code:
t = @async error("boom")
try
    fetch(t)
catch e
    println(typeof(e))
    println(e.task.exception)
end

sections.body:
A `Channel{T}(n)` is a first-in first-out queue that tasks share: `put!(ch, x)`
adds a value, `take!(ch)` removes the oldest one. The number `n` is the buffer
size: `put!` waits when the buffer is full and `take!` waits when it is empty,
which is what lets a fast producer and a slow consumer cooperate. Give the
channel an element type, as with arrays: `Channel(n)` alone is a
`Channel{Any}`, and every value taken out of it has the abstract type `Any`.

`Channel{T}(f, n)` (usually written with `do`) starts a task running `f(ch)`
and **closes** the channel when `f` returns. A `for` loop over a channel takes
values until the channel is closed and empty, so producer/consumer code needs
no explicit end-of-data marker.

examples.code:
ch = Channel{Int}(3)
put!(ch, 10)
put!(ch, 20)
println(take!(ch))
println(isready(ch))   # is there a value waiting?
println(take!(ch))
println(isready(ch))

examples.caption: A producer task; the consumer is the `collect` (or any `for` loop).
examples.code:
squares = Channel{Int}(4) do ch
    for i in 1:5
        put!(ch, i^2)
    end
end   # the channel closes when the do-block returns
collect(squares)

examples.caption: A two-stage pipeline: each stage is a task reading one channel and writing the next. Values keep their order.
examples.code:
numbers = Channel{Int}(8) do ch
    foreach(i -> put!(ch, i), 1:6)
end
doubled = Channel{Int}(8) do ch
    for x in numbers
        put!(ch, 2x)
    end
end
total = 0
for y in doubled
    global total += y
end
total

close(ch)
put!(ch, 1)

sections.body:
Everything so far ran on **one** CPU core: the tasks took turns. That is
*concurrency*, and it is what you want for waiting on many things at once
(downloads, files, user input). *Parallelism* means running at the same
moment on several cores, which speeds up computation.

`Threads.@spawn expr` is like `@async` but lets the scheduler run the task on
any of Julia's threads. How many threads there are is fixed when Julia
starts: `julia -t auto` uses one per CPU core, `julia -t 4` uses four (or set
the environment variable `JULIA_NUM_THREADS`). This site runs your code with
**one thread**, so the spawned tasks below take turns, but the same code runs
in parallel when you start Julia with `-t auto` on your own machine, and it
gives the same answer because results are combined only through `fetch`.
(The practice problem at the end of this unit is graded on four threads.)

sections.title: Concurrency is not parallelism: threads

sections.body:
A **data race** happens when tasks update shared state with a read, then a
write, and another task gets in between. `total[] += 1` is exactly that: read
`total[]`, add 1, write it back. With several threads, two tasks can read the
same old value and one increment is lost, so the result changes from run to
run.

On one thread the tasks only switch at yield points, so the race stays hidden.
The example below makes it visible anyway by yielding between the read and
the write: four tasks each add 1 a thousand times, and the total is 1000, not
4000. (With real threads the lost updates happen without any `yield`.)

Three race-free fixes, from best to worst for speed:

* **Per-task partial results**, combined at the end with `fetch` (the
  `chunked_sum` above). No shared state at all.
* **`Threads.Atomic{Int}`** with `Threads.atomic_add!`: the read-modify-write
  becomes one indivisible hardware operation. Works for plain numbers only.
* **A lock** (`ReentrantLock`), held during the whole read-modify-write with
  `lock(l) do ... end`. Works for anything (a `Dict`, a `push!`), but tasks
  queue up to take turns.

examples.caption: A race made visible on one thread: lost updates.
examples.code:
total = Ref(0)
@sync for i in 1:4
    Threads.@spawn for _ in 1:1000
        t = total[]
        yield()            # another task runs between the read and the write
        total[] = t + 1
    end
end
total[]

examples.caption: The same loop with the read-modify-write inside a lock.
examples.code:
total = Ref(0)
l = ReentrantLock()
@sync for i in 1:4
    Threads.@spawn for _ in 1:1000
        lock(l) do
            t = total[]
            yield()
            total[] = t + 1
        end
    end
end
total[]

examples.caption: An atomic counter: `atomic_add!` returns the old value and adds in one step.
examples.code:
total = Threads.Atomic{Int}(0)
@sync for i in 1:4
    Threads.@spawn for _ in 1:1000
        Threads.atomic_add!(total, 1)
    end
end
total[]

sections.body:
Threads share memory inside one Julia process. Two other kinds of parallelism
are worth knowing about (Distributed ships with Julia and unit 40 starts a worker
with it; no GPU package is installed in this sandbox):

* **Distributed** (a standard library): `addprocs(4)` starts worker
  *processes*, possibly on other machines; `@everywhere` defines code on all of
  them, and `pmap(f, xs)` or `@distributed` share out the work. Workers do not
  share memory, so data is copied to them: worth it for large independent jobs.
* **GPUs**: packages such as CUDA.jl (NVIDIA), AMDGPU.jl and Metal.jl (Apple)
  provide array types that live on the graphics card. Broadcasting and many
  array functions on them run as GPU kernels, and you can write your own
  kernels in Julia.

Whatever the hardware, the rules from this unit carry over: split the work so
that each worker owns its piece, and combine the results at the end.

sections.body:
When you call a function, Julia picks the **method** by the types of all the
arguments (multiple dispatch), and then compiles that method for exactly those
argument types. The compiled version is a **method instance** (a
*specialization*). `double(x) = 2x` is one method, but calling it with an
`Int` and with a `Float64` compiles two separate pieces of machine code, each
as fast as if you had written it for that type by hand.

`methods(f)` lists the methods; `Base.specializations(m)` lists the instances
compiled for method `m` so far (we sort them by name, because the order they
are stored in is not meaningful). `Base.return_types(f, (T,))` asks type
inference what the result type would be for argument type `T`, without
running anything.

examples.code:
double(x) = 2x
double(3)
double(2.5)
println(methods(double))
m = only(methods(double))
sort([string(mi) for mi in Base.specializations(m)])
examples.output:
# 1 method for generic function "double" from Main:
 [1] double(x)
     @ main.jl:1
2-element Vector{String}:
 "MethodInstance for double(::Float64)"
 "MethodInstance for double(::Int64)"

sections.body:
`@code_typed f(args...)` shows the code after type inference and
optimization: each line is one operation with its inferred type after `::`,
and `=> T` at the end is the return type. The `@code_...` macros live in the
`InteractiveUtils` standard library, which the REPL loads for you; in a
script (and on this site) write `using InteractiveUtils` first.

Notice what is *not* there: `2x` for an `Int` became a single
`Base.mul_int` (an integer multiplication), with no dispatch left at run time.
In the unstable `pos`, the two `return` lines have different types; that is
what `@code_warntype` highlights in red at the REPL.

One level further down, `@code_llvm` shows LLVM's intermediate code and
`@code_native` the machine instructions. Their output depends on your CPU
and contains generated names that change between runs, so we only show one
example, unchecked.

examples.caption: Unchecked: the function name in the first line (`julia_double_…`) carries a counter that varies between runs.

sections.title: Reading the compiled code: @code_typed

sections.body:
Two optimizations explain a lot of Julia's speed:

* **Inlining**: a small function's body is pasted into its caller, so the
  call disappears. `x^3` with a literal exponent is turned into two
  multiplications this way.
* **Constant propagation**: when arguments are known constants, inference
  computes with the values, not just the types. Below, `answer()` calls
  `inc(41)`; the optimized code is just `return 42`.

`optimize = false` shows the code before these passes: the call to `inc` is
still there, but inference already knows its result is the constant 42
(`Core.Const(42)`).

examples.code:
using InteractiveUtils
inc(x) = x + 1
answer() = inc(41)
@code_typed answer()

using InteractiveUtils
inc(x) = x + 1
answer() = inc(41)
@code_typed optimize = false answer()

examples.caption: A literal power is inlined into plain multiplications.
examples.output:
CodeInfo(
1 ─ %1 = Base.mul_int(x, x)::Int64
│   %2 = Base.mul_int(%1, x)::Int64
└──      return %2
) => Int64

sections.title: Constant propagation and inlining

sections.body:
Every method definition increments a global counter, the **world age**. A
running function sees the methods that existed in the world where it
started, so the compiled code it is running stays valid. If a function
defines a new method with `@eval` (or `include`) and calls it right away, the
call fails with "method too new to be called from this world context".

`Base.invokelatest(f, args...)` makes the call in the newest world. It is
slower (a dynamic call), so use it at the boundary where code is loaded, not
in an inner loop. At the top level of a script or the REPL each statement
starts in the latest world, which is why this never bites there.

The two world ages in the message are large numbers that depend on how many
methods were defined before, so the course shows them as `W` and `W+1`.

examples.code:
function load_and_call()
    @eval plugin() = "plugin loaded"
    try
        plugin()
    catch e
        println(typeof(e))
    end
    println(Base.invokelatest(plugin))
end
load_and_call()
println(plugin())   # top level: the latest world again

examples.caption: The MethodError says exactly this.

ERROR: MethodError: no method matching newfun()
The applicable method may be too new: running in world age W, while current world is W+1.

Closest candidates are:

   @ Main main.jl:2

  @ define_and_call at line 3
  @ top-level scope at line 5

sections.title: World age: why eval'd methods need invokelatest

sections.body:
Compilation happens the first time each method instance is called, so the
first call is slow and later ones are fast. This is the "time to first x"
(TTFX) you notice when a package's first plot takes seconds. The example
below is unchecked because it prints timings; `@time` reports the share of
compilation time on the first call.

To cut that cost, packages **precompile**: when you install or update one,
Julia stores its compiled code in a cache file (`.ji` plus, since Julia
1.9, native code in a `.so`/`.dll`) so later sessions can load it.
Precompilation workloads (PrecompileTools.jl's `@compile_workload`) run
typical calls at that time so their specializations are cached too.

An **invalidation** happens when a newly loaded method could change what
existing compiled code would call: Julia must throw that code away and
compile it again. Defining `Base.+` for a new combination of Base types (type
piracy) is a classic cause. SnoopCompile.jl finds invalidations and
inference bottlenecks when load times matter.

0.3384236261145569

The **standard library** is a set of packages that come with Julia: you load
them with `using` but never install them. `LinearAlgebra` adds `norm`, `dot`,
`det`, `eigen`, factorizations, and `I`, the identity of whatever size is
needed. Matrix literals separate columns with spaces and rows with `;`, and
`*` on matrices is the matrix product (`.*` is element by element).

To solve `A x = b`, write `A \ b`. It picks a suitable factorization (LU for
a square matrix, QR for a tall one, which gives the least-squares solution)
and is both faster and more accurate than `inv(A) * b`.

Floating-point results from the underlying BLAS/LAPACK libraries can differ
in the last digits between machines, so the examples round them with
`round.(x; digits = 6)`.

using LinearAlgebra

b = [1.0, 2.0]
x = A \ b
println(round.(x; digits = 6))
println(A * x ≈ b)                        # ≈ compares with a tolerance
println(round(det(A); digits = 6), " ", round(norm([3.0, 4.0]); digits = 6), " ", dot([1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]))

For reproducible results, create a random number generator with a seed and
pass it as the first argument: `rand(rng, ...)`, `randn(rng, ...)`,
`shuffle(rng, v)`, `randperm(rng, n)`. The same seed gives the same
sequence. `Xoshiro` is Julia's default generator.

Be aware that the numbers a given seed produces may change between Julia
versions (they are only guaranteed within a release). For data that must stay
the same forever, such as test fixtures, use a package like StableRNGs.jl.
Functions that need randomness should take the generator as an argument, so
callers (and tests) can control it.

examples.code:
using Random
rng = Xoshiro(1234)
println(rand(rng, 1:6, 5))      # five dice rolls
println(rand(rng, 1:6, 5))      # the generator moved on: different rolls
println(rand(Xoshiro(1234), 1:6, 5) == rand(Xoshiro(1234), 1:6, 5))

using Random
rng = Xoshiro(7)
println(shuffle(rng, 1:6))
println(randperm(rng, 6))
println(round.(randn(rng, 3); digits = 4))

`Date` is a calendar day, `DateTime` a day plus a time to the millisecond.
Arithmetic uses *periods* such as `Day(1)`, `Month(1)`, `Hour(12)`;
subtracting two dates gives a number of days. `dayofweek` numbers days from
Monday = 1 to Sunday = 7. A range of dates, `d1:Day(1):d2`, iterates over
every day in between.

`Date("2024-12-25")` parses ISO dates; for other layouts give a format,
written with the `dateformat"..."` string macro so it is parsed only once:
`y` year, `m` month number, `u` abbreviated month name, `d` day, `H` hours,
`M` minutes.

examples.code:
using Dates
d = Date(2024, 2, 28)
println(d + Day(1), " ", d + Day(2))     # 2024 is a leap year
println(Date(2024, 3, 1) - d)
println(dayofweek(d), " ", dayname(d))
println(d + Month(1))

using Dates
dt = DateTime(2024, 3, 10, 14, 30)
println(dt + Hour(12))
println(Dates.format(dt, dateformat"dd u yyyy, HH:MM"))
println(Date("25/12/2024", dateformat"dd/mm/yyyy"))

examples.caption: Count the Saturdays in March 2024 with a range of dates.
examples.code:
using Dates
march = Date(2024, 3, 1):Day(1):Date(2024, 3, 31)
count(d -> dayofweek(d) == Saturday, march)

`@printf` and `@sprintf` (from `Printf`) format numbers C-style: `%.3f`
three decimals, `%5d` an integer padded to width 5, `%-6s` a left-aligned
string, `%e` scientific notation, `%08.2f` zero padding. The format is
checked when the macro expands.

`Test` is how Julia packages are tested. `@test expr` passes when `expr` is
`true`; `@test a ≈ b` compares floats with a tolerance (never use `==` on
computed floats); `@test_throws T expr` passes when `expr` throws a `T`.
`@testset` groups tests and prints a summary. The summary normally has a
`Time` column; `showtiming = false` removes it, which we need here so the
output is the same on every run. A failing `@test` outside a testset is an
error that shows the expression and its evaluated value.

examples.code:
using Printf
@printf("%.3f|%5d|%-6s|%e\n", pi, 42, "ab", 12345.678)
s = @sprintf("%08.2f", 3.14159)
s

using Test
@test 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3
